Opening

title: Basics of NLP
heading: What is Natural Language Processing?
text:
Every technique in this course is a different answer to the middle box: how to turn words into numbers without losing what matters.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field
of Artificial Intelligence that studies how computers can
process, understand, analyze, and generate human language.

Human language is not a table of numbers. It is text and speech
produced by people: messages, questions, news, documents,
reviews, voice commands. NLP is the set of methods that turns
this material into something a computer can work with — and then
turns the result back into language a person can read.

The basic flow

Human Language
→

Natural Language Processing
→

Understanding / Classification / Search / Generation

Concept

title: Basics of NLP
heading: Why is NLP difficult?
text:
The first three are properties of language itself. The fourth is a property of Kazakh specifically, and it changes which methods are practical.

A programming language has one grammar and no exceptions. Human
language has neither. It is:

Ambiguous

The same word can mean different things.

Contextual

Meaning depends on the sentences around it.

Multilingual

One message can mix several languages.

Constantly changing

New words, slang, and abbreviations appear all the time.

Culture-dependent

Politeness, irony, and references are local.

Morphologically rich

In Kazakh, one root produces a very large number of surface
forms.

Ambiguity

Kazakh example
Ол банкте отыр.

Without context, at least two readings are possible:

the person works at a bank

the person is physically sitting inside a
bank

A human resolves this from the situation. A model has to learn
it from context.

Morphology

Kazakh is an agglutinative language: suffixes are added one after
another. The same root appears in many surface forms.

One root, many forms

кітап
book
кітаптар
books
кітаптарым
my books
кітаптарымыздан
from our books

For a computer these are four completely different strings.
Making them comparable is exactly the job of Tokenization and
Lemmatization, which we meet later in the course.

Multilingual reality

A realistic message in Kazakhstan

Сәлем, meeting сағат 15:00-де болады, Teams-ке кіресің бе?

In one short sentence we already have:

Kazakh grammar and word order

English terminology ( meeting ,
Teams )

numbers and time formats

punctuation and Kazakh suffixes attached to English words

title: Basics of NLP
heading: The evolution of NLP
text:
Each step did not delete the previous one — it added a new way of
representing language. Our course roughly follows this path.

Rules →

Machine Learning →

Transformers →

BERT / GPT →

Large Language Models →

RAG / Agents

when we have the vocabulary for it.

Motivation

title: Regular Expressions
heading:
Before models understand language, we first need to work with
text.
text:
Every NLP pipeline starts with plain, messy text: extra spaces,
phone numbers, dates, hashtags, mixed languages. The oldest and
still the most used tool for that first pass is:

Regular Expressions — Regex

Definition

title: Regular Expressions
heading: What are Regular Expressions?
text:
Regular Expressions are patterns used to find,
extract, validate, split, or replace text.

The engine slides along the text and retries the pattern at every position. A match is nothing more than a starting point and a length.

Text
+

Pattern
=

Match

A Regex does not understand meaning. It only describes
shape . And every pattern is built from just four
kinds of piece — which is exactly how we will go through them:

1
What character?

Character classes: \d , \w , [абв]

2
How many times?

Quantifiers: + , * , ? , {n}

3
This or that?

Alternation and groups: | , ( )

4
Where exactly?

Anchors: ^ , $ , \b

Building block 1

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Character classes — what character?
text:
A character class matches one character. This is
the smallest piece of every pattern.

A class is a menu, and the engine picks exactly one item from it per match. Two vowels in «салем» means two separate one-character matches.

Character classes with examples

Pattern
Matches one…
Example

\d
digit 0-9
\d\d\d → 701

\D
character that is not a digit
\D → the space in +7 701

\w
word character (letter, digit, _ )
#\w+ → #Astana

\s
whitespace: space, tab, newline
\s → the gap between words

\S
anything that is not whitespace
\S+ → one whole word

.
any character at all
А.тана → Астана

[абв]
one of the listed characters
[АӘ] → А or Ә

[^абв]
anything except those
[^0-9] → any non-digit

[а-я]
a range of characters
[A-Z] → K in KZK

Kazakh letters are a range too

The Kazakh alphabet adds letters that plain
[а-я] does not cover. Write them in
explicitly:

[а-яёәғқңөұүһі]

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Quantifiers — how many times?
text:
A quantifier repeats the piece written directly before it.

Blue cells are required, grey ones optional. Adding ? after a quantifier makes it lazy: it stops at the first chance instead of the last.

Quantifiers with examples

Pattern
Means
Example

+

\d+ → 2026

*

\s* → matches even if there is no space

?

https? → http and https

{4}

\d{4} → 1991

{2,4}

\d{2,4} → 12 , 123 , 1234

{3,}

\d{3,} → 7172

Result:

http://egov.kz

Piece by piece http these four letters, exactly as written s? an optional s — ? means “zero or one”, and it applies only to the single character in front of it :// three more literal characters \S+ one or more characters that are not whitespace — the rest of the address In words: http, maybe an s, then :// , then everything up to the next space. Detail: \S+ stops only at a space, so in Сайт https://astana.kz. Келесі… it also swallows the final dot and returns https://astana.kz. — a good reminder that “until the next space” is not the same as “until the end of the link”. title: Regular Expressions
heading: Quantifiers — how many times?
text:

In words: find a < , then some characters, then a > — and the only difference is how far “some characters” reaches.

Why it happens: a greedy + first runs to the very end of the text, then walks backwards until the rest of the pattern fits. The last > in the line fits, so it keeps everything. The lazy version starts short and grows only when it has to, so it settles on the first > .

Building block 3

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Alternation and groups — this or that?
text:
| has the lowest precedence in the whole language, so it splits everything around it. Brackets are how you tell it where to stop.

Alternation: | means OR

Any of several cities

Астана, Алматы және Шымкент — үлкен қалалар.

Pattern: Астана|Алматы|Шымкент

Result:

Астана

Алматы

Шымкент

Piece by piece

Астана
the first alternative
|
OR — the engine tries the alternatives left to right and takes the first one that fits at that position
Алматы
the second alternative
Шымкент
the third alternative

In words: at this position, match Астана, or Алматы, or Шымкент.

Watch the scope: | splits the whole pattern, not just the word next to it. ^Астана|Алматы means “Астана at the start” OR “Алматы anywhere”, so in Астанада Алматы бар it finds both. Wrap the alternatives in brackets — ^(?:Астана|Алматы) — and only Астана at the start matches.

Groups: ( ) keep things together

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Alternation and groups — this or that?
text:
бар it finds both. Wrap the alternatives in brackets — ^(?:Астана|Алматы) — and only Астана at the start matches.

Groups: ( ) keep things together

Brackets do two jobs at once: they decide what a quantifier or an
| applies to, and they
capture the matched piece so you can read it back.

Capturing the parts of a date

Кездесу 24.08.2026 күні өтеді.

Pattern: (\d{2})\.(\d{2})\.(\d{4})

whole match
24.08.2026
group 1 — day
24
group 2 — month
08
group 3 — year
2026

Groups turn “find a date” into “find a date and take it
apart ”.

Piece by piece

(
opens group 1 — groups are numbered by the order of their opening brackets
\d{2}
exactly two digits — the day
)
closes group 1
\.
an escaped dot: a real dot character, not “any character”
(\d{2})
group 2 — the month
(\d{4})
group 3 — the year

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Alternation and groups — this or that?
text:
igits — the day
)
closes group 1
\.
an escaped dot: a real dot character, not “any character”
(\d{2})
group 2 — the month
(\d{4})
group 3 — the year

In words: two digits, a dot, two digits, a dot, four digits — and remember each number block separately.

Detail: the whole match is always available as group 0, and the captured pieces start at 1. In Python that is m.group(0) , m.group(1) , … — but careful: re.findall returns the groups instead of the whole match as soon as the pattern has any, which is why the next example uses non-capturing brackets.

Grouping without capturing

(?:…) groups without keeping the
result — useful when you only need the brackets for structure:

Билет 1 500 теңге, кофе 990 тг, тағы бірі 12 000 теңге.

Pattern:
\d+(?:\s\d{3})*\s*(?:теңге|тг)

Result:

1 500 теңге

990 тг

12 000 теңге

Piece by piece

\d+
one or more digits — matches 990 , or the 1 of 1 500

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Alternation and groups — this or that?
text:
\d+(?:\s\d{3})*\s*(?:теңге|тг)

Result:

1 500 теңге

990 тг

12 000 теңге

Piece by piece

\d+
one or more digits — matches 990 , or the 1 of 1 500
(?:
opens a group that is not captured — brackets used only for structure
\s\d{3}
a space followed by exactly three digits — one thousands block, like 500
)*
zero or more of those blocks: none for 990 , one for 1 500 , one for 12 000
\s*
an optional space before the currency word
(?:теңге|тг)
either spelling of the currency, again without capturing

In words: a number, possibly written with spaces between thousands, followed by теңге or тг.

Why (?:…) and not (…) : with plain brackets, re.findall would return only what the brackets caught — ['теңге', 'тг'] — instead of the whole price. Non-capturing brackets give the grouping without changing what you get back.

Building block 4

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Anchors and boundaries — where exactly?
text:
Anchors match a position , not a character. They
consume nothing; they only say “here”.

The blue and red bars sit between the letters, not on them. That is what “zero-width” means — an anchor never uses up a character.

^ start of the text

^Астана matches only if the text
begins with that word.

$ end of the text

\.$ matches a final full stop.

\b word boundary

\b\d{4}\b matches
2017 as a standalone number, not
four digits inside a longer one.

\B not a boundary

The opposite of \b — useful for
finding something inside a word.

A trap worth remembering. In JavaScript
\b is defined through
\w , which is ASCII only. So
\bАстана\b matches
nothing in a browser, while the same pattern
works in Python. With Kazakh or Russian text, either drop the
\b , or switch on the
u flag and use
\p{L} for “any letter”.

Unicode-safe patterns

Бүгін #Astana және #Астана туралы жаздық.

#\w+

Building block 5

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Escaping — when a character means itself
text:
These characters have a special job inside a pattern:

Without the backslash, . matches any character at all — so the pattern would also accept text that is not a domain.

. + * ? ( ) [ ] { } | ^ $ \

To match one of them literally, put a backslash in front of it.

Escaped characters

Wrong
Right
Why

\d{2}.\d{2}
\d{2}\.\d{2}
a bare . matches any character, so 24x08 would pass

+7
\+7
a bare + means “one or more” and needs something before it

(2026)
\(2026\)
brackets create a group instead of matching brackets

Inside [ ] most characters lose their
special meaning, which is why
[\w.-] needs no escaping for the dot.
In Python, re.escape("+7 (701)") escapes
a string for you.

Putting it together

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
Every pattern below is only the building blocks from above, put
next to each other.

Example 01 · Phone numbers
Kazakhstan phone numbers

Менің нөмірім +7 701 123 45 67.
Кеңсе: +7 7172 55 44 33.

Pattern: \+7[\s\d]+

+7 701 123 45 67

+7 7172 55 44 33

Piece by piece

\+
an escaped plus — a bare + would mean “one or more” and would need something in front of it
7
the digit 7, literally
[\s\d]
one character that is either whitespace or a digit
+
one or more of those characters

In words: a literal +7 , then any run of digits and spaces.

Where it stops: at the first character that is neither a space nor a digit — the full stop after 67 , or the comma after 33 . Its weakness: it never counts digits, so +7 701 123 45 67 2026 жылға gives +7 701 123 45 67 2026 — the year gets swallowed. \+7(?:[\s-]?\d){10} counts ten digits and stops in the right place.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
701 123 45 67 2026 жылға gives +7 701 123 45 67 2026 — the year gets swallowed. \+7(?:[\s-]?\d){10} counts ten digits and stops in the right place.

Production-grade validation would need stricter rules — this
pattern happily accepts nonsense like
+7 999999999999 .

Example 02 · Years
Extract years

Қазақстан тәуелсіздігін 1991 жылы алды.
EXPO 2017 Астанада өтті.

Pattern: \b\d{4}\b

1991

2017

Boundary + class + quantifier: three pieces, one useful
pattern.

Piece by piece

\b
a word boundary — the position between a word character and a non-word character
\d{4}
exactly four digits
\b
another word boundary, on the other side

In words: four digits standing on their own.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
aracter and a non-word character
\d{4}
exactly four digits
\b
another word boundary, on the other side

In words: four digits standing on their own.

Why the boundaries matter: without them, \d{4} applied to нөмір 12345 happily returns 1234 — the first four digits of a longer number. With \b on both sides there is no match at all, which is what you want when you are looking for years.

Example 03 · Dates
Extract dates

Кездесу 24.08.2026 күні Астанада өтеді.

Pattern: \b\d{2}\.\d{2}\.\d{4}\b

24.08.2026

Piece by piece

\b
word boundary, so we do not start in the middle of a longer number
\d{2}
the day — exactly two digits
\.
an escaped dot: the separator itself
\d{2}
the month
\.
the second separator
\d{4}
the year — exactly four digits
\b
closing word boundary

In words: two digits, dot, two digits, dot, four digits — the Kazakhstan date format.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
\d{4}
the year — exactly four digits
\b
closing word boundary

In words: two digits, dot, two digits, dot, four digits — the Kazakhstan date format.

The classic mistake: writing \d{2}.\d{2}.\d{4} without escaping. A bare . matches any character, so that pattern also accepts 24x08y2026 . Also note: the pattern checks the shape, not the calendar — 99.99.2026 would pass.

Example 04 · Time
Extract times of day

Кездесу сағат 15:00-де, кеші 9:05-те аяқталады.

Pattern:
\b(?:[01]?\d|2[0-3]):[0-5]\d\b

15:00

9:05

Alternation inside a non-capturing group lets us say “00–19 or
20–23”, so 25:99 is rejected.

Piece by piece

(?:
a non-capturing group holding the two hour options
[01]?\d
an optional 0 or 1, then any digit → covers 0–9 and 00–19
|
or
2[0-3]
a 2 followed by 0–3 → covers 20–23
:
the literal colon
[0-5]\d
minutes: first digit 0–5, then any digit → 00–59

|
or
2[0-3]
a 2 followed by 0–3 → covers 20–23
:

[0-5]\d
minutes: first digit 0–5, then any digit → 00–59

In words: an hour from 0 to 23, a colon, then minutes from 00 to 59.

What the ranges buy you: a lazy \d{1,2}:\d{2} would also accept 25:99 . Here the alternation encodes the real rule, so 25:99 is rejected while both 15:00 and the single-digit 9:05 are accepted.

Example 05 · Vehicle plates
Kazakhstan vehicle plates

123 ABC 01
777 KZK 02

Pattern: \d{3}\s[A-Z]{3}\s\d{2}

123 ABC 01

777 KZK 02

Real plate formats and their validation rules are more complex
than this; the pattern shows fixed-length groups.

Piece by piece

\d{3}
exactly three digits
\s
exactly one whitespace character
[A-Z]{3}
exactly three capital Latin letters
\s
another single space
\d{2}
exactly two digits — the region code

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
\s
exactly one whitespace character
[A-Z]{3}
exactly three capital Latin letters
\s
another single space
\d{2}
exactly two digits — the region code

In words: three digits, space, three capital letters, space, two digits.

Detail: {3} is strict — no more, no less. And [A-Z] is Latin only, so a plate typed with Cyrillic А or В (which look identical on screen) will not match. Confusable letters are a genuine, everyday problem in Kazakhstan text data.

Example 06 · Hashtags
Find hashtags

Бүгін #Astana қаласында #AI туралы конференция өтті.

Pattern: #\w+

#Astana

#AI

For Kazakh hashtags use
#[^\s#]+ — see the anchors section.

Piece by piece

#
a literal hash character
\w
one word character — a letter, a digit or an underscore
+
one or more of them, so the tag runs until the first space or punctuation

In words: a hash, then the run of word characters after it.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
underscore
+
one or more of them, so the tag runs until the first space or punctuation

In words: a hash, then the run of word characters after it.

The Kazakh catch: in JavaScript \w is only [A-Za-z0-9_] , so #Астана is missed entirely. Use #[^\s#]+ (“a hash, then anything that is not a space or another hash”), or switch on the u flag and write #[\p{L}\d_]+ .

Example 07 · Cleaning
Clean extra spaces

Алматы Қазақстанның ең ірі қалаларының бірі.

Pattern: \s+ — replacement:
" "

Алматы Қазақстанның ең ірі қалаларының бірі.

Normalising whitespace is one of the very first steps of
almost every text-processing pipeline.

Piece by piece

\s
one whitespace character — a space, a tab, or a newline
+
one or more in a row, so a run of ten spaces is a single match
" "
the replacement: exactly one ordinary space

In words: replace every run of whitespace with a single space.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
run of ten spaces is a single match
" "
the replacement: exactly one ordinary space

In words: replace every run of whitespace with a single space.

Why + matters here: without it you would replace each space with a space and change nothing. With it, the whole run collapses at once. In Python this is re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text) , and .strip() afterwards removes the leftover space at the start and end.

Example 08 · Emails
Extract email addresses

Сұрақтарды info@example.kz адресіне жіберіңіз.

Pattern: [\w.-]+@[\w.-]+\.\w+

info@example.kz

Piece by piece

[\w.-]
one character that is a word character, a dot, or a hyphen
+
one or more of them — the part before the @
@
the literal at sign
[\w.-]+
the same set again — the domain name
\.
an escaped dot before the zone
\w+
the zone itself: kz , com , …

In words: some name characters, an @, some domain characters, a dot, and a zone.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Regex with Kazakhstan data
text:
.
an escaped dot before the zone
\w+
the zone itself: kz , com , …

In words: some name characters, an @, some domain characters, a dot, and a zone.

Two details worth knowing. Inside [ ] the dot loses its special meaning, so it needs no backslash there — but outside the brackets it does. And the hyphen is written last on purpose: in the middle it would create a range, as in a-z .

This is not a complete, RFC-compliant email validator. It is
good enough to find addresses in text, which is
usually what an NLP pipeline actually needs.

title: Regular Expressions
heading: Practising in Python
text:
In the practical part of NLP work we use Python. Every output
below is the real output of the code above it — run them yourself
and change the text.

1 · findall — every match at once

import re

text = "Қазақстан 1991 жылы тәуелсіз болды. EXPO 2017 Астанада өтті."
years = re.findall(r"\b\d{4}\b", text)

print(years)

['1991', '2017']

What happens here: findall scans the whole string and returns every match as a list of strings. If nothing matches you get an empty list, not None — so you can loop over the result safely. The gotcha: as soon as your pattern contains capturing brackets, findall returns the contents of the brackets instead of the whole match.

2 · search + groups — take a match apart

import re

text = "Кездесу 24.08.2026 күні өтеді."
m = re.search(r"(\d{2})\.(\d{2})\.(\d{4})", text)

print(m.group(0))
print(m.groups())
print("Year:", m.group(3))

24.08.2026

print("Year:", m.group(3))

Year: 2026

What happens here: search looks for the first match only and gives you a Match object — group(0) is everything that matched, group(1) , group(2) , … are the bracketed pieces, numbered by their opening bracket. Always check for None : if nothing matches, search returns None and m.group(0) raises AttributeError .

3 · Named groups — readable code

import re

text = "Курс 24.08.2026 күні басталады."
m = re.search(
r"(?P<day>\d{2})\.(?P<month>\d{2})\.(?P<year>\d{4})",
text
)

print(m.groupdict())
print(m.group("month"))

{'day': '24', 'month': '08', 'year': '2026'}
08

What happens here: (?P<day>…) gives a group a name, so the code says m.group("month") instead of m.group(2) — and stays correct even if you later insert another bracket. groupdict() hands you all named groups as a dictionary, ready to build a date object. Note the syntax difference: Python writes (?P<name>…) , JavaScript writes (?<name>…) .

4 · sub — clean the text

import re

text = "Алматы Қазақстанның ең ірі қалаларының бірі."
clean = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

print(clean)

What happens here: sub replaces every match, not just the first, and returns a new string — the original is untouched, because Python strings are immutable. \s+ collapses each run of whitespace into one space; .strip() then removes the space that may be left at the very start and end.

5 · sub — remove punctuation before tokenizing

import re

text = "Сәлем, әлем! Бүгін #NLP сабағы бар."
words_only = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", "", text)

print(words_only)

What happens here: [^\w\s] reads as “not a word character and not whitespace” — that is, punctuation and symbols. Replacing it with an empty string leaves words and the spaces between them. Why it works on Kazakh: Python’s \w is Unicode-aware, so Сәлем counts as word characters. The same line in JavaScript would delete every Cyrillic letter instead.

\w is Unicode-aware. The same pattern
in JavaScript would delete every Cyrillic letter — always check
which engine you are in.

6 · Prices — alternation and optional blocks

import re

text = "Билет 1 500 теңге, кофе 990 тг, тағы бірі 12 000 теңге."
prices = re.findall(r"\d+(?:\s\d{3})*\s*(?:теңге|тг)", text)

print(prices)

print(prices)

What happens here: all the brackets are non-capturing, so findall returns whole prices rather than pieces of them. (?:\s\d{3})* is what makes 1 500 and 12 000 work while still matching plain 990 — “zero or more thousands blocks”.

7 · finditer — matches with their positions

import re

text = "Бүгін #Astana қаласында #AI туралы конференция өтті."

for m in re.finditer(r"#\w+", text):
print(m.group(), m.start(), m.end())

#Astana 6 13
#AI 24 27

What happens here: finditer returns Match objects instead of strings, so you also get start() and end() — the character positions of each match. You need those whenever the position matters: highlighting a match in a page, replacing it in place, or storing an entity span for Named Entity Recognition, which is exactly the format NER training data uses.

Positions matter as soon as you want to highlight a match, replace

8 · split — cut text into sentences

import re

text = "Астана — астана. Алматы ірі қала! Шымкент те үлкен?"
sentences = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text)

print(sentences)

['Астана — астана.', 'Алматы ірі қала!', 'Шымкент те үлкен?']

What happens here: split cuts the string wherever the pattern matches and returns the pieces. The lookbehind (?<=[.!?]) checks that a sentence mark is directly behind the current position without consuming it, so the punctuation stays attached to its sentence and only the space between sentences is used as the cut point.

after a . ,

9 · compile + flags — reuse one pattern

import re

nlp = re.compile(r"\bnlp\b", re.IGNORECASE)

print(nlp.findall("NLP, nlp, Nlp курсы"))

What happens here: re.compile builds the pattern once and gives you an object with the same methods — findall , search , sub . Use it when the same pattern runs over many texts; it also keeps the flags in one place. re.IGNORECASE makes NLP , nlp and Nlp all match.

10 · A small pipeline

Regex is rarely used alone — it is the cleaning step in front of
everything else.

import re

raw = " Сәлем!!! Менің нөмірім +7 701 123 45 67, #NLP "

phones = re.findall(r"\+7[\s\d]+", raw) # keep what we need
text = re.sub(r"\+7[\s\d]+", "<PHONE>", raw) # then anonymise it
text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip() # normalise whitespace

print(phones)
print(text)

['+7 701 123 45 67']
Сәлем!!! Менің нөмірім <PHONE>, #NLP

What happens here — and why in this order: first findall keeps a copy of the phone numbers, because the next line destroys them; then sub replaces each number with <PHONE> , which is how personal data is removed from a dataset before training; only then is the whitespace normalised, so the extra spaces left behind by the replacement disappear too. Swap the first two lines and you lose the numbers.

That pattern is still fragile. [\s\d]+
means “spaces and digits, as many as possible”, so in
+7 701 123 45 67 2026 жылға дейін it
swallows the year as well and returns
+7 701 123 45 67 2026 . A pattern that
counts the digits —
\+7(?:[\s-]?\d){10} — stops in the
right place. Always look at what your Regex
actually matched.

How this lecture is organised. First the theory
— the whole pipeline, step by step. Then the practice — an
interactive lab, Python code you can run, and exercises.

Four steps, and each one is a deliberate loss. The last column is the only thing a classical model ever sees.

A Machine Learning model cannot read a sentence. It reads
vectors of numbers . Text Processing is the

The whole pipeline in one function

Everything above, written out. Run it and you get exactly the vector from the table — the same nine numbers.

import re
from collections import Counter

VOCAB = ['алматыда', 'астанада', 'ауа', 'бүгін', 'емес',
'жауды', 'жақсы', 'жаңбыр', 'райы']

def pipeline(text):
text = text.lower()
text = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", text)
return text.split()

raw = " Астанада ауа райы ЖАҚСЫ!!! "
tokens = pipeline(raw)
counts = Counter(tokens)

print("tokens:", tokens)
print("vector:", [counts[w] for w in VOCAB])

tokens: ['астанада', 'ауа', 'райы', 'жақсы']
vector: [0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1]

Read the last line: the vector is built against a fixed vocabulary, so position 2 always means астанада and position 7 always means жақсы . Change the vocabulary and every stored vector becomes meaningless — which is why the vectorizer must be saved together with the model.

Theory · Step 1

title: Text Processing
heading: Normalization — making text comparable
text:
Normalization brings text that means the same
thing into the same written form, so that a computer comparing
strings sees them as equal.

Case

Астана and
АСТАНА are different strings until
you lowercase them.

Whitespace

Tabs, double spaces and line breaks collapse into one space —
the \s+ pattern from Lecture 1.

Punctuation

жақсы!!! and
жақсы should usually count as the
same word.

Unicode

The same letter can be stored in two ways; NFC normalization
makes them identical byte for byte.

What this looks like in practice

Three cleaning steps

What we just lost: the hashtag

marks — a strong signal for Sentiment Analysis — are gone. For

Kazakh needs extra care

Traps specific to our texts

Two scripts. The same word may arrive in
Cyrillic ( Астана ) or in Latin
( Astana ). To a vectorizer these are
two unrelated terms.

Look-alike letters. Cyrillic
А, В, С, Е, О, Р are visually
identical to Latin A, B, C, E, O, P
but have different codes — the same problem we saw with
vehicle plates.

Kazakh-only letters.
ә ғ қ ң ө ұ ү һ і are sometimes
typed as а г к н о у у х и by
people without a Kazakh keyboard.

The letter і. Kazakh
і (U+0456) and Latin

The letter і. Kazakh

None of this is exotic — it is what Kazakhstan text data
actually looks like, and it is why normalization is never
“just .lower() ”.

How to keep what cleaning would destroy

The fix for the problem above: pull the signals out before you clean, and rewrite the hashtag so tokenization cannot swallow it.

import re

raw = "Сәлем, ӘЛЕМ!!! Бүгін #NLP сабағы бар."

# 1. save the signals BEFORE cleaning destroys them
features = {
"exclamations": raw.count("!"),
"hashtags": re.findall(r"#\w+", raw),
"has_shouting": bool(re.search(r"\b[А-ЯЁӘҒҚҢӨҰҮҺІA-Z]{3,}\b", raw)),
}

# 2. keep the hashtag as one token instead of losing the #

The pattern to remember: extract first, clean second. exclamations and has_shouting become ordinary numeric features next to the word counts, and hashtag_nlp survives as a single token that a classifier can learn separately from the word nlp .

How to repair mixed scripts

And the fix for the Cyrillic/Latin traps: normalize to NFC, then map the look-alike Latin letters onto their Cyrillic twins.

And the fix for the Cyrillic/Latin traps: normalize to NFC, then map the look-alike Latin letters onto their Cyrillic twins.

import unicodedata

# Latin letters that look identical to Cyrillic ones, both cases
LOOKALIKE = str.maketrans({
"A": "А", "B": "В", "C": "С", "E": "Е", "H": "Н", "I": "І",
"K": "К", "M": "М", "O": "О", "P": "Р", "T": "Т", "X": "Х",
"a": "а", "c": "с", "e": "е", "i": "і", "o": "о", "p": "р",
"x": "х", "y": "у",
})

def fix_script(text):
return unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text).translate(LOOKALIKE)

cyrillic = "Астана"
mixed = "A" + "стана" # the first letter is Latin A

print(cyrillic == mixed)
print(fix_script(mixed) == cyrillic)
print(fix_script("Ipi"), fix_script("Ipi") == "Ірі")

title: Text Processing
heading: Tokenization — cutting text into units
text:
The same sentence, three tokenizers. Each row keeps something the row above lost, and the third only exists because someone decided prices and room counts mattered.

Tokenization splits text into
tokens — the smallest units the model will
count. A token is usually a word, but it does not have to be.

Attempt 1 — split on spaces

The simplest tokenizer

text = "Сәлем, әлем! Бүгін NLP сабағы бар."
print(text.split())

['Сәлем,', 'әлем!', 'Бүгін', 'NLP', 'сабағы', 'бар.']

The problem is visible immediately:
Сәлем, and Сәлем are now two different
tokens, and so are бар. and бар . The
vocabulary doubles for no reason.

Words only

Sentence tokenization

Splitting into sentences is a separate task, and the naive
“split at every dot” fails on abbreviations and initials —
А. Құнанбайұлы is not two sentences. We
already met the careful version in Lecture 1 with a lookbehind.

How to protect what you do not want split

The answer to the 15:00 problem: replace the structured pieces with placeholders first, using the Regex patterns from Lecture 1, and only then split into words.

text = re.sub(r"\+7(?:[\s-]?\d){10}", " <PHONE> ", text)

import re

def protect(text):
text = re.sub(r"\+7(?:[\s-]?\d){10}", " <PHONE> ", text)
text = re.sub(r"\b\d{2}\.\d{2}\.\d{4}\b", " <DATE> ", text)
text = re.sub(r"\b\d{1,2}:\d{2}\b", " <TIME> ", text)
text = re.sub(r"#(\w+)", r" hashtag_\1 ", text)
return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()

raw = "Сәлем, meeting 15:00-де, 24.08.2026 күні. Тел: +7 701 123 45 67 #NLP"

print(protect(raw))
print(re.findall(r"<\w+>|\w+", protect(raw)))

['Сәлем', 'meeting', '<TIME>', 'де', '<DATE>', 'күні', 'Тел', '<PHONE>', 'hashtag_NLP']

Two wins at once. The time, the date and the phone number survive as single tokens instead of exploding into digits, and the phone number is anonymised on the way — the same line does feature engineering and privacy work. Placeholders also shrink the vocabulary: every phone number in the corpus becomes one column, not thousands.

How to keep hyphenated names together

One tokenizer, three rules in order: a hyphenated Cyrillic name, then a plain word of either script, then numbers.

import re

KAZ = "А-ЯЁӘҒҚҢӨҰҮҺІа-яёәғқңөұүһі"
TOKEN = re.compile(rf"[{KAZ}]+(?:-[{KAZ}]+)+|[{KAZ}]+|[A-Za-z]+|\d+")

text = "Қасым-Жомарт Тоқаев Teams-ке кірді"
print(TOKEN.findall(text))

['Қасым-Жомарт', 'Тоқаев', 'Teams', 'ке', 'кірді']

[{KAZ}]+|[A-Za-z]+|\d+")

text = "Қасым-Жомарт Тоқаев Teams-ке кірді"
print(TOKEN.findall(text))

['Қасым-Жомарт', 'Тоқаев', 'Teams', 'ке', 'кірді']

Қасым-Жомарт stays one token because the first alternative is tried first, while Teams-ке still splits — the hyphen there joins two different scripts, which is exactly the case we do want split. Alternation order is the whole trick: put the longest, most specific rule first.

How to split sentences without breaking on initials

The naive splitter cuts after А. The guard hides the dot of a single-letter initial, splits, then puts it back.

import re

text = "Абай А. Құнанбайұлы — ақын. Ол 1845 жылы туған! Солай ма?"

naive = re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", text)
print("naive :", naive)

guarded = re.sub(r"\b([А-ЯЁӘҒҚҢӨҰҮҺІ])\.\s", r"\1<DOT> ", text)
parts = [p.replace("<DOT>", ".") for p in re.split(r"(?<=[.!?])\s+", guarded)]

Theory · Step 2b

title: Text Processing
heading: Subword tokens — why modern models split words
text:
Kazakh has a problem that English does not: one root produces an
enormous number of surface forms, so a word-level vocabulary
never stops growing.

One root, many entries

For a word-level vocabulary these are five unrelated terms:

кітап

кітаптар

кітаптарым

кітапхана

кітаптарымыздан

Multiply that by every noun in the language and the vocabulary
explodes. Worse, a form the model never saw during training is
simply unknown — the out-of-vocabulary problem.

The modern answer is to make the tokens smaller than words. A
subword tokenizer learns frequent character
sequences from the data and splits rare words into known pieces:

кітаптарымыздан
→

кітап
+

тар
+

ымыз
+

дан

An illustration, not a real model output. The
exact pieces depend on the corpus the tokenizer was trained on.
The important idea is that an unseen word is still representable,

exact pieces depend on the corpus the tokenizer was trained on.
The important idea is that an unseen word is still representable,
because its parts are known. BPE (used by GPT
models) and WordPiece (used by BERT) are the two
algorithms you will meet again in the Transformers lectures.

For today we stay with word-level tokens: they are what Bag of
Words needs, and they are easy to inspect by eye.

BPE in twenty lines

Not a real tokenizer, but the real algorithm: start from single characters, then repeatedly merge the most frequent neighbouring pair.

words = ["кітап", "кітаптар", "кітаптарым", "кітаптарымыздан"]
corpus = {" ".join(word) + " </w>": 1 for word in words}

def best_pair(corpus):
pairs = Counter()
for word, freq in corpus.items():
symbols = word.split()
for i in range(len(symbols) - 1):

rge 1: 'т' + 'а' (seen 7x)
merge 2: 'к' + 'і' (seen 4x)
merge 3: 'кі' + 'та' (seen 4x)

Watch what the algorithm discovers. Nobody told it about Kazakh morphology, yet after four merges it has learned кітап as a unit — because that sequence keeps repeating. Continue the loop and the suffixes тар , ымыз , дан emerge the same way. That is how a subword vocabulary is built from data alone.

Theory · Step 3

title: Text Processing
heading: Stemming and Lemmatization
text:
Stemming cuts by rule, lemmatization looks the word up. Both collapse many forms into one column — which is the point, and also the loss.

Both answer the same question: how do we make
кітап and
кітаптарымыздан count as one thing?

Stemming

Cuts the ending off by rules. Fast, crude, and the result is
often not a real word: English studies →
studi .

Lemmatization

Returns the lemma — the dictionary form —
using a dictionary and grammar: studies →
study , кітаптарым →
кітап .

Why naive stemming fails in Kazakh

“Just cut three characters”

forms = ["кітап", "кітаптар", "кітаптарым", "кітаптарымыздан"]
print([f[:-3] for f in forms])

['кі', 'кітап', 'кітапта', 'кітаптарымыз']

Four different results for one root. The rule
destroys the short word ( кітап → кі )
and barely touches the long one. Correct lemmatization returns
кітап for all four.

The morphology behind it

title: Text Processing
heading: Stemming and Lemmatization
text:
destroys the short word ( кітап → кі )
and barely touches the long one. Correct lemmatization returns
кітап for all four.

The morphology behind it

кітаптарымыздан, piece by piece

Suffix by suffix

кітап
the root — “book”
-тар
plural
-ымыз
possessive, “our”
-дан
ablative case, “from”

In words: “from our books” — one Kazakh word
where English needs three.

And the suffixes themselves change shape. The
ablative appears as -дан , -ден ,
-тан , -тен , -нан or
-нен depending on the sounds before it — vowel
harmony and consonant assimilation. A list of endings is not
enough; you need a morphological analyser.

Practical note. For English, stemming is often
good enough. For Russian there are mature analysers. For Kazakh
the tooling is thinner — which is exactly why subword tokenization
is so attractive for agglutinative languages, and why Kazakh NLP
is an open field for your own work.

A suffix stripper that actually works

The fix for the “cut three characters” disaster: try the longest suffixes first, strip repeatedly, and never let the stem get shorter than four characters.

SUFFIXES = ["ымыздан", "імізден", "ларымыз", "леріміз", "тарымыз",
"дан", "ден", "тан", "тен", "нан", "нен",
"лар", "лер", "тар", "тер", "дар", "дер",
"ым", "ім", "ың", "ің", "да", "де", "та", "те"]

def strip_suffixes(word, min_stem=4):
changed = True
while changed:
changed = False
for suffix in sorted(SUFFIXES, key=len, reverse=True):
if word.endswith(suffix) and len(word) - len(suffix) >= min_stem:
word = word[: -len(suffix)]
changed = True
break
return word

for form in ["кітап", "кітаптар", "кітаптарым", "кітаптарымыздан", "қалалар"]:

for form in ["кітап", "кітаптар", "кітаптарым", "кітаптарымыздан", "қалалар"]:

кітап → кітап
кітаптар → кітап

All four forms now collapse to кітап , and қалалар to қала . But be honest about the limits: the list ignores vowel harmony variants you forgot to add, and it will happily damage a word that merely ends in those letters. It is a decent baseline, not a morphological analyser — treat every result as a guess to be checked.

Theory · Step 4

title: Text Processing
heading: Stopwords — removing the filler
text:
Stopwords are very frequent words that carry
little meaning on their own: және ,
бұл , ол ,
и , в ,
the , of .

Before and after

import re

STOP = {"және", "бұл", "ол", "да", "де", "мен", "бен"}

text = "Астана және Алматы бұл үлкен қалалар"
tokens = re.findall(r"\w+", text.lower())
kept = [w for w in tokens if w not in STOP]

print("tokens:", tokens)
print("kept :", kept)

tokens: ['астана', 'және', 'алматы', 'бұл', 'үлкен', 'қалалар']
kept : ['астана', 'алматы', 'үлкен', 'қалалар']

Six tokens became four, and nothing important was lost — for a
topic classifier.

Now the dangerous case. Many Kazakh stopword
lists contain емес — “not”. Remove it
and ауа райы жақсы емес (“the weather
is not good”) becomes
ауа райы жақсы — the exact opposite.
For Sentiment Analysis that single deletion inverts the label.

Rules of thumb: remove stopwords for topic classification and
keyword search, keep them for sentiment, negation, question
detection, and anything where grammar matters. And always look at
the list before you use it.

How to remove stopwords without losing negation

The fix for the dangerous case: take the stopword list you were given, subtract the words that carry negation, and use the difference.

import re

STOP = {"және", "бұл", "ол", "да", "де", "мен", "бен", "емес", "жоқ"}
NEGATION = {"емес", "жоқ", "ешқашан"}
SAFE_STOP = STOP - NEGATION

text = "тамақ дәмді емес және қымбат"
tokens = re.findall(r"\w+", text.lower())

print("naive :", [w for w in tokens if w not in STOP])
print("safe :", [w for w in tokens if w not in SAFE_STOP])

naive : ['тамақ', 'дәмді', 'қымбат']

safe : ['тамақ', 'дәмді', 'емес', 'қымбат']

One line — SAFE_STOP = STOP - NEGATION — saves the label. The naive version returns дәмді (“tasty”) for a sentence that says the opposite. Build the same guard for question words if you classify questions, and for pronouns if you do coreference.

Theory · Step 5

title: Text Processing
heading: Bag of Words — the first vector
text:
One row per document, one column per vocabulary word. Rows 2 and 3 are byte-identical, which is the flaw this course spends three more lectures fixing.

Bag of Words represents a document as a count
of its words. You build a vocabulary of every term in the
collection, then each document becomes a row of counts — one
column per term. Word order is thrown away; that is why it is a
“bag”.

Worked example — three sentences

D1: Астанада ауа райы жақсы
D2: Алматыда ауа райы жақсы емес
D3: Астанада бүгін жаңбыр жауды

D1: ['астанада', 'ауа', 'райы', 'жақсы']
D2: ['алматыда', 'ауа', 'райы', 'жақсы', 'емес']
D3: ['астанада', 'бүгін', 'жаңбыр', 'жауды']

Step 2 — collect the vocabulary (every distinct
term, sorted):

['алматыда', 'астанада', 'ауа', 'бүгін', 'емес', 'жауды', 'жақсы', 'жаңбыр', 'райы']

Measuring how similar two vectors are

This is what a model actually does with those rows — cosine similarity, the angle between two documents.

import re, math
from collections import Counter

docs = ["Астанада ауа райы жақсы",
"Алматыда ауа райы жақсы емес",
"Астанада бүгін жаңбыр жауды"]

tokens = [re.findall(r"\w+", d.lower()) for d in docs]
vocab = sorted({w for t in tokens for w in t})
vectors = [[Counter(t)[w] for w in vocab] for t in tokens]

def cosine(a, b):
dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
return dot / (math.sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a)) * math.sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b)))

print("D1 vs D2:", round(cosine(vectors[0], vectors[1]), 3))
print("D1 vs D3:", round(cosine(vectors[0], vectors[2]), 3))

D1 vs D2: 0.671
D1 vs D3: 0.25

print("D1 vs D3:", round(cosine(vectors[0], vectors[2]), 3))

D1 vs D2: 0.671
D1 vs D3: 0.25

D1 and D2 come out 67% similar even though one says the weather is good and the other says it is not, while D1 and D3 — both about Astana — score only 0.25. Bag of Words measures shared vocabulary, not shared meaning. Remember this number when we add bigrams.

Theory · Step 6

title: Text Processing
heading: TF-IDF — not all words are equally useful
text:
The bars show how many documents contain each word. IDF is the inverse: a word in every document distinguishes nothing, so its weight collapses.

In raw counts, a word that appears in every document weighs as
much as a word that appears in one. But the rare word is what
makes a document distinctive.

TF-IDF multiplies how often a term appears in
this document by how rare it is across
all documents.

TF — term frequency

How often the term occurs in this document, usually divided by
the document length:
tf = count / total tokens

IDF — inverse document frequency

How rare the term is in the collection:
idf = ln(N / df) , where
df is the number of documents
containing it.

The same three sentences, in numbers

алматыда: 1 емес: 1 бүгін: 1 жаңбыр: 1 жауды: 1

IDF:

ln(3/2) = 0.405 → ауа, райы, жақсы, астанада

Which words carry each document

Ranking every term by its TF-IDF weight shows what the vectorizer thinks each document is about.

import re, math
from collections import Counter

docs = ["Астанада ауа райы жақсы",
"Алматыда ауа райы жақсы емес",
"Астанада бүгін жаңбыр жауды"]

tokens = [re.findall(r"\w+", d.lower()) for d in docs]
vocab = sorted({w for t in tokens for w in t})
N = len(docs)

df = {w: sum(1 for t in tokens if w in t) for w in vocab}
idf = {w: math.log(N / df[w]) for w in vocab}

for i, t in enumerate(tokens, 1):
counts = Counter(t)
scores = {w: counts[w] / len(t) * idf[w] for w in set(t)}
top = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[:2]
print(f"D{i} top terms:", [(w, round(s, 3)) for w, s in top])

D2 is characterised by алматыда and емес — precisely the two words that distinguish it. The sort key is (-score, term) rather than -score alone: several terms tie here, and without the tie-breaker the output order would change between runs.

Theory · Step 7

title: Text Processing
heading: N-grams — putting a little order back
text:
Bigrams keep жақсы емес together as one feature, so the negation survives — at the price of a much wider vocabulary.

An n-gram is a sequence of n neighbouring
tokens. Counting bigrams (n = 2) instead of, or alongside,
single words gives the model a small window of context.

Bigrams of D2

import re

tokens = re.findall(r"\w+", "Алматыда ауа райы жақсы емес".lower())
bigrams = [" ".join(pair) for pair in zip(tokens, tokens[1:])]

print(bigrams)

['алматыда ауа', 'ауа райы', 'райы жақсы', 'жақсы емес']

There it is: жақсы емес is now a
single feature. A classifier can learn that this bigram means
something different from жақсы — the negation
problem from the Bag of Words section is solved, at least for
neighbouring words.

The price. Vocabulary grows fast: a corpus with
50 000 distinct words has up to 2.5 billion possible bigrams. In

The price. Vocabulary grows fast: a corpus with
50 000 distinct words has up to 2.5 billion possible bigrams. In
practice you keep only bigrams that occur often enough —
min_df in scikit-learn — and accept that longer
dependencies (“ жақсы деп айтуға болмайды ”) stay
out of reach until we have models that read sequences.

Keeping only the bigrams that earn their place

This is min_df by hand: count in how many documents each bigram appears, and keep those seen at least twice.

import re
from collections import Counter

docs = ["ауа райы жақсы емес",
"бүгін ауа райы жақсы",
"ертең ауа райы жақсы болады"]

def bigrams(tokens):
return [" ".join(pair) for pair in zip(tokens, tokens[1:])]

tokens = [re.findall(r"\w+", d.lower()) for d in docs]
doc_freq = Counter()
for t in tokens:
doc_freq.update(set(bigrams(t)))

Theory · The honest summary

title: Text Processing
heading: What Bag of Words cannot do
text:
Order is gone

Shuffle the words of a sentence and its vector does not change
at all. Kazakh case suffixes still separate
ит адамды қапты from
адам итті қапты — until
Lemmatization strips exactly those suffixes.

Meaning is gone

дәрігер and
емші are as unrelated to the model
as дәрігер and
трактор — different columns, no
connection.

Unknown words are invisible

A word missing from the vocabulary simply does not exist. In
an agglutinative language that happens constantly.

Vectors are huge and empty

A vocabulary of 50 000 terms gives every short message a
50 000-long vector where almost every value is zero.

Bag of Words
→

TF-IDF
→

Word Embeddings
→

Transformers

Each arrow fixes a limitation of the step before it. Embeddings
give words that share meaning similar vectors; Transformers bring
back the order. But TF-IDF is still a strong, cheap baseline —

Seeing the losses in code

Three print statements that make the limitations concrete.

from collections import Counter

d1 = ["астанада", "ауа", "райы", "жақсы"]
shuffled = ["жақсы", "райы", "астанада", "ауа"]
print("same vector after shuffling:", Counter(d1) == Counter(shuffled))

# In Kazakh the case suffixes still separate the roles …
a = ["ит", "адамды", "қапты"] # the dog bit the man
b = ["адам", "итті", "қапты"] # the man bit the dog
print("raw tokens differ :", Counter(a) != Counter(b))

# … until lemmatization strips exactly those suffixes
lemma = {"адамды": "адам", "итті": "ит"}
la = [lemma.get(w, w) for w in a]
lb = [lemma.get(w, w) for w in b]

raw tokens differ : True

Line 1: shuffle a sentence and the vector does not change at all. Lines 2 and 3 are the interesting ones: in Kazakh the case suffixes -ды and -ті mark who bit whom, so the raw vectors still differ — Kazakh survives Bag of Words better than English does. But lemmatization strips exactly those suffixes, and the two sentences become identical. Two steps of the pipeline, each sensible alone, together destroy the meaning.

import re

def normalize(text):
text = text.lower()
text = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", text)
text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)
return text.strip()

raw = " Сәлем, ӘЛЕМ!!! Бүгін #NLP сабағы бар. "

Five questions to answer together before we finish.

Question 1

Name the steps that turn " Астанада ауа райы ЖАҚСЫ!!! " into a vector, in order.

Show Answer

Normalization → Tokenization → (Lemmatization) →

Question 2

Why does cutting three characters off every word fail for Kazakh?

Show Answer

Because the suffixes have different lengths and change shape
with vowel harmony. The rule destroys кітап
(→ кі ) and leaves
кітаптарымыздан almost untouched — one root
ends up as four different features.

Question 3

D1: ауа райы жақсы
D2: ауа райы жақсы емес

The vectors differ by a single count, because word order and

Question 4

A term appears in all three documents. What is its idf, and what does that mean?

Show Answer

ln(3/3) = ln(1) = 0 , so its TF-IDF weight is
zero in every document. A word that is everywhere
distinguishes nothing — TF-IDF removes it automatically,
without any stopword list.

Theory · Why bother

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Why classical algorithms, in the age of LLMs?
text:
Because for a great many real tasks they are still the right answer —
and because everything that comes later is easier to understand once
you have seen a model learn from counted words.

They need little data

Eight thousand reviews and a laptop are enough to reach 0.784 on
this task. For most languages other than English, datasets of that
size are what you actually have.

They are readable

You can print the exact words behind every decision. Try
explaining a refused loan application with “the neural network
said so”.

They are cheap and fast

Training takes seconds on a laptop, prediction takes
microseconds, and deployment is a file of numbers — no GPU.

They are the baseline

You cannot claim a large model helps until a TF-IDF baseline has
been beaten. Surprisingly often, it has not been.

The honest limit. These models see only the words you

heading: Why classical algorithms, in the age of LLMs?
text:
arge model helps until a TF-IDF baseline has
been beaten. Surprisingly often, it has not been.

The honest limit. These models see only the words you
counted. Word order, meaning and context are still out of reach —
everything Lecture 2 warned about. When the task needs those, the later
lectures are where you go.

Theory · The map

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: The supervised learning pipeline
text:
Supervised learning means learning from examples
that already carry the right answer. You give the model pairs of
(text, label); it finds the pattern that connects them.

Labelled text →

TF-IDF features →

Train / test split →

Model →

Metrics →

Error analysis

The last arrow points back to the first box. Error analysis tells you
what to change — usually the data, not the algorithm — and you go
round again. That loop is the actual job.

Algorithm 1

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Naive Bayes
text:
Naive Bayes asks a simple question: which class was
most likely to have produced these words? It multiplies the
probability of each word given each class, and picks the winner.

The rule behind it is Bayes' theorem, with one bold simplification:

P(class | words) ∝ P(class) × P(word₁ | class) × P(word₂ | class) × …

The simplification — the “naive” part — is that the words are assumed
independent of each other. That is plainly false in
language: жақсы and
емес are not independent. The model works
anyway, which is one of the pleasant surprises of the field.

Two details that make it work

Logarithms

Multiplying hundreds of small probabilities underflows to zero, so
we add logarithms instead. That is why the scores below are
negative numbers.

Smoothing

A word never seen with a class would give probability 0 and wipe out
the whole product. Laplace smoothing adds

The whole model, in six lines

A Pipeline chains the vectorizer and the classifier into one
object. That matters: the same vocabulary and the same weighting are
applied at training and at prediction time, which is where hand-written
pipelines usually go wrong.

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

model = Pipeline([
("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2, sublinear_tf=True)),
("clf", MultinomialNB(alpha=1.0)),
])
model.fit(x_train, y_train)

Algorithm 2

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Logistic Regression
text:
Logistic Regression gives every word a weight,
adds up the weights of the words present, and squeezes the total into
a probability between 0 and 1. Training means adjusting the weights
until the predictions match the labels.

z = w₁·x₁ + w₂·x₂ + … + b P(class) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ)

positive

negative

Every document is a point; the model looks for a straight line that
separates the classes. In reality the space has one dimension per
word — thousands of them — but the picture is the same.

Compared with Naive Bayes it drops the independence assumption: weights
are fitted together , so a word that only matters next to
another one can be down-weighted. It usually wins on larger datasets,
and it gives calibrated probabilities you can threshold.

The one parameter you will actually tune.
C controls regularisation: small C keeps the
weights small and the model simple, large C lets it fit the

text:

The one parameter you will actually tune.
C controls regularisation: small C keeps the
weights small and the model simple, large C lets it fit the
training data closely — and overfit. Start at C=1 and move
by factors of ten.

Algorithm 3

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Support Vector Machines
text:
An SVM also draws a line — but not just any line. It
looks for the one with the widest empty corridor around it, the
margin . Only the points on the edge of that corridor
matter; they are the support vectors .

The shaded corridor is the margin. The two outlined points are the
support vectors — move any other point and the boundary does not
change at all.

For text this matters: with thousands of sparse features, many
separating lines fit the training data perfectly, and the widest-margin
one generalises best. LinearSVC is often the strongest
classical baseline for text classification.

Linear kernel, always — for text. The RBF kernel is
famous, but on high-dimensional sparse text data it is slower and rarely
better. Use LinearSVC . Its one drawback: it gives no
probabilities, only decisions — if you need a confidence score, use
Logistic Regression.

Algorithms 4 and 5

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: k Nearest Neighbours, trees and forests
text:
kNN — no training at all

kNN stores the training set and, for a new document, finds the
k most similar ones — cosine similarity from
Lecture 2 — and takes a vote.

The cross is a new review. Inside the circle: two positive
neighbours and one negative, so the vote says positive.

The cost moves. There is nothing to train, but every
prediction compares the new review against all 8 000 training reviews.
On this dataset that makes kNN far slower than Naive Bayes at prediction
time, for no gain in accuracy — the reason it is rarely used for text.

Decision trees and random forests

A decision tree asks yes/no questions —
“does the review contain нашар ?” — and follows
the branches to a class. A single tree overfits badly; a
random forest trains hundreds of them on random subsets
and averages the votes.

And this is what they actually score here. The single
tree is the weakest model in the lecture — 0.750 on the test set, 0.732
under cross-validation, with double the fold-to-fold variance of the
linear models. The forest repairs most of that (0.775) but still does not
catch Naive Bayes, while fitting almost perfectly on the training data
(0.980) and taking five times longer.

Why they struggle. A tree splits on one feature at a
time, and a TF-IDF matrix has 9 419 sparse columns where almost every
value is zero. Use trees for text when you combine words with other
features — review length, rating history, time of day — because mixing
feature types is exactly what they are good at.

Theory · Measuring

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Metrics: accuracy is not enough
text:
Precision

Of everything the model called negative, how much really was? Punishes false alarms.

Recall

Of all the real negative reviews, how many did it find? Punishes misses.

F1

The harmonic mean of the two — one number when you must have one number.

Confusion matrix

Which class is mistaken for which. The only one that tells you what to fix.

From the run above: negative precision 0.782, recall 0.787. The two are
nearly equal, which means the model is not trading one for the other — it
simply misses about a fifth of the complaints and raises about as many
false alarms. Whether that is acceptable depends on which mistake costs
more.

Negative recall collapses from 0.787 to 0.154. Trained

Theory · Trusting the number

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: How much data, and how much trust
text:
Two questions worth asking about any reported accuracy: would more data
improve it, and how much would it move if you had split differently?

More data

from lesson3 import load, balance, build

train_raw = load("train")
test = balance(load("test"), 1000)
x_test, y_test = test["text_cleaned"].astype(str), test["label"]

for per_class in (250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000):
train = balance(train_raw, per_class)
model = build("nb")
model.fit(train["text_cleaned"].astype(str), train["label"])
print(f"{2 * per_class:>5} training reviews → accuracy {model.score(x_test, y_test):.3f}")

1000 training reviews → accuracy 0.746
2000 training reviews → accuracy 0.773
4000 training reviews → accuracy 0.779
8000 training reviews → accuracy 0.784

Sixteen times more data buys five points, and the curve is flattening.

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text

4000 training reviews → accuracy 0.779
8000 training reviews → accuracy 0.784

Sixteen times more data buys five points, and the curve is flattening.
That is the shape to expect from a bag-of-words model: it climbs quickly,
then stalls, because it never learns that two different word forms mean
the same thing. Breaking through that ceiling needs different features,
not more rows.

Cross-validation

A single test score is one sample. Five-fold cross-validation splits the
training data five ways and trains five times, for every model:

for name in ("nb", "logreg", "svm", "tree", "forest"):
scores = cross_val_score(build(name), x, y, cv=5)

its own fold-to-fold spread — that is what makes the ranking believable.

Theory · A common trap

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Class imbalance
text:
Real data is never balanced. KazSAnDRA is 82% positive; a fraud
dataset might be 99.9% clean. The rare class is usually the one you care
about.

Weight the classes

class_weight="balanced" in scikit-learn makes each
mistake on a rare class count more. One parameter, usually the first
thing to try.

Resample

Drop examples of the frequent class, or duplicate the rare one. Cheap,
and it throws away information or invites overfitting — respectively.

Move the threshold

With Logistic Regression you decide the cut-off yourself: predict
“fraud” at probability 0.2 rather than 0.5 when a miss is expensive.

Report the right metric

Use macro-F1 or per-class recall. Accuracy on imbalanced data is a
number that makes everyone comfortable and tells no one anything.

Theory · Looking inside

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text

Every model here can be asked which features push hardest towards each
class. On real reviews this is the fastest way to find out whether it
learned sentiment or something else.

model = build("logreg")
model.fit(train["text_cleaned"].astype(str), train["label"])

print("positive:", ", ".join(positive))

түсініксіз (unclear) against жақсы (good),
рахмет (thanks), ыңғайлы (convenient).

69% of the vocabulary appears exactly once. Nineteen
thousand distinct forms from seventy-two thousand tokens — the model sees
most words a single time and can learn almost nothing from them. This is

en
thousand distinct forms from seventy-two thousand tokens — the model sees
most words a single time and can learn almost nothing from them. This is
the morphology lesson from Lecture 2 arriving as a number: every case and
possessive suffix creates another form that Bag of Words treats as an
unrelated word.

Three problems, all visible in the data

Morphology splits the evidence. The frequent words
are the ones that resist inflection — өте (very),
жақсы (good), керемет (great). Anything
inflected is scattered across forms.

Reviews are very short. A median of six words, 23%
with three or fewer. «Әлі қатады го» carries almost no
signal for a word-counting model.

The text is mixed. Russian words
( регистрация , реклама , ужас )
sit inside Kazakh sentences, exactly the code-switching from
Lecture 0 — and they are among the most predictive features.

In class

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Knowledge check
text:
Five questions to answer together before we finish.

Question 1

KazSAnDRA is 82% positive. Why did we balance it, and what would accuracy mean if we had not?

Show Answer

On the raw distribution a model that always answers “positive”
scores 0.82, so accuracy no longer separates a working model from a
useless one. After balancing, 0.500 is the coin flip and 0.784 is
real. We measured the cost of not balancing: negative recall falls
from 0.787 to 0.154.

Question 2

What exactly is "naive" about Naive Bayes, and why does it still work here?

Show Answer

It assumes words are independent given the class, which is false for
language. For classification only the ranking matters — the right
class needs the highest score, and the probabilities themselves can
be badly wrong.

Question 3

Negative precision is 0.825 but recall is 0.735. Explain the difference to a product manager.

Show Answer

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Knowledge check
text:
hemselves can
be badly wrong.

Question 3

Negative precision is 0.825 but recall is 0.735. Explain the difference to a product manager.

Show Answer

When the system flags a review as a complaint, it is right about
83% of the time. But it only catches 74% of the real complaints —
one in four is missed. Which number matters depends on whether a
false alarm or a missed complaint costs more.

Question 4

Cross-validation gives 0.792 ± 0.006, the single test split gives 0.784. Which do you report?

Show Answer

Roughly 0.78, and say which set it came from. Cross-validation uses
only training data, the test split is held out, and the small
difference between them is well inside the fold-to-fold spread. Never
report the higher of two numbers without saying how it was measured.

Question 5

«Жақсы бəрін көруге болады» is labelled negative; the model says positive. Who is wrong?

Show Answer

title: Classical Machine Learning for Text
heading: Knowledge check
text:
thout saying how it was measured.

Question 5

«Жақсы бəрін көруге болады» is labelled negative; the model says positive. Who is wrong?

Show Answer

Probably the label. Real datasets contain annotation noise, and part
of every accuracy gap belongs to the data rather than the model.
Before tuning anything, read a sample of the errors and estimate how
many are actually label problems.

title: Word Embeddings
heading: By the end of this lecture you can…
text:
Explain an embedding

Say what a word vector is, where it comes from, and what “close together” means.

Train your own

Use gensim to train word2vec and fastText on real text, and save them.

Use them as features

Load the saved models back and replace TF-IDF in the Lecture 3 classifier.

Know the limits

Explain what a static vector cannot represent, and what comes after.

Train first, reuse second. Most of this lecture is
about producing embeddings and looking at them. Only at the end do we load
them back into the classifier of Lecture 3 — same task, same split, same
classifier, with the features being the one thing that changed.

Theory · The core idea

title: Word Embeddings
heading: What an embedding is
text:
A model cannot read. Everything it does is arithmetic, so a word has to
become numbers before anything else can happen. Lectures 2 and 3 turned
words into numbers by counting them. This lecture turns them into
numbers by placing them.

Step 1 — a word becomes a list of numbers

Two numbers place a point on a sheet of paper. Three place it in a room.
One hundred place it in a space nobody can picture — but the arithmetic
for “how far apart are these two points” works exactly the same in all
three cases. That is the whole trick: give every word a fixed-length list
of numbers, and questions about meaning turn into questions about
position.

An embedding is a list of numbers attached to a word —
its coordinates. Every word gets a list of the same length (100 numbers
in this lecture), and the lists are chosen so that words used in similar
ways end up in similar places.

Step 2 — closeness is an angle

Once words are points, “do these two words mean similar things?” becomes
“do these two points lie in the same direction?” The measure is the cosine
similarity from Lecture 2 — the same formula, applied to word vectors
instead of document vectors.

How to read a cosine

+1 the same direction — used in the same way
0 at right angles — nothing in common
-1 opposite directions

Step 4 — where the numbers come from

Nobody types them in, and there is no dictionary involved. Every word
starts with 100 random numbers — a meaningless space — and those numbers
are then corrected millions of times:

Give every word in the vocabulary 100 random numbers.

Slide a small window along the text and take a pair: a word and one of
the words actually standing next to it.

Ask the current numbers a question — judging by these coordinates,
does this pair look like a real neighbour pair?

The answer is usually wrong, so nudge the two vectors a little towards
each other. Take a few pairs that never occur together and nudge those
apart.

Repeat for every position in the corpus, ten times over.

No one labelled anything. The text supplies both the question (a word) and

Repeat for every position in the corpus, ten times over.

No one labelled anything. The text supplies both the question (a word) and
the answer (its real neighbours), which is why plain, unlabelled Kazakh
text is enough — and why the millions of unlabelled sentences on the
internet suddenly become useful.

Words that keep appearing next to the same neighbours get nudged towards
the same region over and over, so they end up close together. That is the
entire mechanism, and the rest of this lecture is its detail: which pairs
are chosen, how the nudge is computed, what breaks for a language like
Kazakh, and whether any of it improves the classifier from Lecture 3.

Theory · The problem

title: Word Embeddings
heading: What TF-IDF cannot do
text:
Three limitations followed us out of Lecture 2, and Lecture 3 measured
the cost of all of them.

Synonyms are strangers

жақсы and
керемет are two unrelated columns. A
review that says one gives the model nothing about the other.

Unseen words vanish

A word missing from the training vocabulary is simply dropped. In
Kazakh, where 69% of the vocabulary appeared exactly once, that
happens constantly.

Vectors are huge and empty

9 419 features for 8 000 short reviews, almost all zeros. Most of the
matrix carries no information at all.

Nothing transfers

Everything the model knows comes from labelled data. The millions of
unlabelled Kazakh sentences on the internet are wasted.

Embeddings attack all four. They are learned from raw text with no labels,
they are dense and small, they give related words related vectors, and —

title: Word Embeddings
heading: What TF-IDF cannot do
text:
Embeddings attack all four. They are learned from raw text with no labels,
they are dense and small, they give related words related vectors, and —
with fastText — they can build a vector for a word they have never seen.

Theory · The idea

title: Word Embeddings
heading: The distributional hypothesis
text:
You shall know a word by the company it keeps. Words
that appear in similar contexts tend to mean similar things — so if we
can describe a word by its neighbours, we have described its meaning.

The same slot, two words
Қосымша өте ______ екен, рахмет!
жақсы
керемет

Both words fit. Across a whole corpus, жақсы
and керемет keep turning up in the same
slots — next to өте , next to
рахмет , in reviews with five stars. Nothing
else needs to be known about them for a model to notice they belong
together.

A schematic view of 100 dimensions squeezed into two. The cosine values
are the real ones, measured later on this page.

Theory · The model

title: Word Embeddings
heading: word2vec
text:
word2vec (Mikolov and colleagues, 2013) turns the distributional
hypothesis into a prediction task. The vectors are not the goal of the
training — they are what is left behind once the task is learned.

Two ways round the same idea

Skip-gram

Given the centre word, predict the words around it. Slower, and
better on small corpora and rare words — which is why we use it here.

CBOW

Given the surrounding words, predict the centre one. Faster, and
smoother on frequent words. In gensim: sg=0 .

Skip-gram with a window of two: from жақсы ,
predict the four words around it. Every position in the corpus becomes
a training example.

How it actually trains

Predicting one word out of a 27 000-word vocabulary would need a
27 000-way softmax at every step, which is far too slow.
Negative sampling replaces it with a much cheaper

title: Word Embeddings
heading: word2vec
text:

27 000-way softmax at every step, which is far too slow.
Negative sampling replaces it with a much cheaper
question: is this pair of words a real neighbour pair, or one I invented?

(жақсы, өте) →

real — push the vectors together

(жақсы, банк) →

invented — push them apart

A handful of invented pairs per real pair is enough. The vectors start
random and are nudged, pair by pair, until words that share company sit
near each other. Nobody ever tells the model what
жақсы means.

What the parameters mean.
vector_size — how many numbers per word; 100–300 is normal.
window — how far “context” reaches; small windows capture
syntax, large ones capture topic. min_count — ignore words
rarer than this. epochs — how many passes over the corpus;
small corpora need more.

Practice · The corpus

title: Word Embeddings
heading: Preparing the corpus
text:
Training needs one thing: a list of sentences, each already split into
words. No labels, no annotation, no cleaning beyond lowercasing.

We use the KazSAnDRA reviews from Lecture 3, but this time we take
all of them and ignore the label column
entirely. Lecture 3 could only use the 8 000 reviews of its balanced
training split, because a classifier needs answers to learn from. An
embedding does not, so all 134 368 are useful here.

import re

split="train", token=os.getenv("HF_TOKEN")).to_pandas()

TOKEN = re.compile(r"\w+")

def tokenize(text):
return TOKEN.findall(str(text).lower())

corpus = [tokenize(text) for text in reviews["text_cleaned"].astype(str)]

print("reviews :", len(corpus))

Why the tokenizer is this simple.
\w+ keeps runs of letters and digits and throws away
everything else. It is the same rule the classifier will use later, and
that matters more than sophistication: if the embeddings are trained on
one kind of token and looked up with another, most lookups miss.

Practice · Training

title: Word Embeddings
heading: Training word2vec with gensim
text:
gensim is the standard Python library for this. It takes the list of
tokenized sentences and gives back a lookup table of vectors.

import os
import re

from dotenv import load_dotenv

load_dotenv(".env")

from datasets import load_dataset
from gensim.models import Word2Vec

reviews = load_dataset("issai/kazsandra", "polarity_classification",
split="train", token=os.getenv("HF_TOKEN")).to_pandas()
corpus = [re.findall(r"\w+", str(text).lower())
for text in reviews["text_cleaned"].astype(str)]

word2vec = Word2Vec(
corpus,
vector_size=100, # numbers per word
window=5, # words of context on each side
min_count=3, # ignore words seen fewer than three times
sg=1, # 1 = skip-gram, 0 = CBOW
epochs=10, # passes over the corpus
workers=1, # one thread, so two runs give the same vectors
seed=42,
)

os.makedirs("models", exist_ok=True)
word2vec.save("models/word2vec.model")

Theory · The upgrade

title: Word Embeddings
heading: fastText and subwords
text:
word2vec has one hard limit: a word it never saw has no vector at all.
For an agglutinative language that is severe — every case and possessive
suffix creates a new form.

fastText represents a word as the sum of its character
n-grams. кітаптарымыздан is built from
кіт , ітап ,
тары , дан and the
rest — so a form that never appeared in training still gets a sensible
vector, assembled from pieces that did.

With min_n=3, max_n=5 , every substring of length 3 to 5
becomes a piece of the word.

Training it is the same call

Same corpus, same settings, two extra parameters — and a second file on
disk next to the first.

Four words, four vectors of 100 numbers, one average of 100 numbers. The
review is now a single point in the same space as the words, and a
classifier can be trained on points.

Averaging throws the order away again. We are back to a
bag of words, only with better words. жақсы емес and
емес жақсы produce exactly the same document vector. The
bigrams of Lecture 2 fixed that for counts; for embeddings the fix is a
model that reads sequences, which is where the course goes next.

Better schemes exist — weighting by idf , SIF with common
component removal, doc2vec — but on this data plain averaging was the
strongest of the ones we tried. Weighting by idf actually
lowered accuracy — 0.787 for word2vec and 0.789 for fastText,

def balance(df, per_class, seed=42):
parts = [g.sample(per_class, random_state=seed) for _, g in df.groupby("label")]
return pd.concat(parts).sample(frac=1, random_state=seed).reset_index(drop=True)

What changed, review by review

164 fixed, 140 broken. The headline gain of 24 reviews

the answer on 304 reviews and only came out 24 ahead. This is what a small
accuracy improvement usually looks like from the inside, and it is why a
single accuracy number is a poor way to decide that one model is “better”.

sentiment word. They lose on short reviews built around one strong word,
because averaging dilutes it. That is a description of when to use which,
and it is more useful than the accuracy column.

text:
Everything on this page comes from
code_files/lesson4.py . It stands
on its own — it loads the data, trains both models, saves them, and only
at the end loads them back for the classifier.

pip install -r requirements.txt # adds gensim

python3 lesson4.py # train, explore, reuse
python3 lesson4.py --retrain # ignore models/ and train again
python3 lesson4.py --dim 200 --epochs 20 # bigger vectors, longer training

The first run trains both models and takes about a minute; it writes
models/word2vec.model and models/fasttext.model ,

--retrain whenever you change --dim ,
--epochs or --min-count — otherwise the old
vectors are loaded under the same name and the new settings do nothing.

Five questions to answer together before we finish.

Question 1

Embeddings are trained without any labels. Where does the training signal come from?

Show Answer

From the text itself: the model predicts which words appear near
which. The corpus supplies both the question and the answer, which
is why unlabelled Kazakh text is suddenly useful.

Question 2

word2vec skipped 2 156 tokens of the test set and fastText skipped none. Why?

Show Answer

word2vec only knows whole words it saw in training. fastText stores
character n-grams, so it can assemble a vector for any string —
including inflected forms it has never met.

title: Text Classification
heading: What every model so far has thrown away
text:
very model in Lectures 2, 3 and 4 sees these two sentences as one input.

Four words, two meanings, one input.
қосымша өте жақсы емес is a complaint;
shuffling the same four words is not. Every representation we have built
collapses them into the same row of numbers, so no classifier trained on
top could ever separate them — the information was destroyed before the
classifier ran. The difference of 3 × 10⁻⁸ is the order in which
the floats were summed, nothing more.

This lecture is about the fix. Instead of collapsing the
review into one point, we feed the words in one at a time and let the model
keep a running summary. Order is then part of the computation rather than
something discarded before it starts.

Theory · The model

title: Text Classification
heading: What a recurrent network is
text:
One small network, applied once per word, carrying a summary of everything
it has read so far.

A recurrent neural network keeps a
hidden state : a vector that starts at zero and is
rewritten at every word, h = f(h, word) . The same
f and the same weights run at every position. After the
last word, that one vector is the model's summary of the review.

The same network drawn four times, not four networks. Its weights are shared across positions, so a review of three words and one of forty go through exactly the same parameters.

Inside a single step

Everything happens in one line of arithmetic. The step takes two things —
the state from the previous word and the current word — multiplies each by
its own weight matrix, adds them together, and squashes the result.

title: Text Classification
heading: What a recurrent network is
text:
ngs —
the state from the previous word and the current word — multiplies each by
its own weight matrix, adds them together, and squashes the result.

One step of a plain RNN. W is applied to the word, U to the previous state; the two are added and squashed by tanh into the new state.

Reading hₜ = tanh(W·xₜ + U·hₜ₋₁ + b)

xₜ
the current word, as its embedding vector — 100 numbers in our model
hₜ₋₁
what the network knew after the previous word — 128 numbers
W, U
the two weight matrices. They are the same at every position: this is what "recurrent" means
tanh
squashes every number into (−1, 1), which stops the state from growing without limit
hₜ
the new state, which becomes hₜ₋₁ at the next word

Reading: there is no memory anywhere else. Whatever the
network wants to remember about the first word has to survive inside
h , through every rewrite that follows.

The clearest way to see it is to run the recurrence by hand and check the
