import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)

# A tiny RNN so the numbers fit on the page: 3-dimensional words, 4-dimensional state.
rnn = nn.RNN(input_size=3, hidden_size=4, batch_first=True)

words = torch.tensor([[[1.0, 0.0, 0.0], # қосымша
[0.0, 1.0, 0.0], # өте
[0.0, 0.0, 1.0], # жақсы
[1.0, 1.0, 0.0]]]) # емес

# --- what nn.RNN does, written out ----------------------------------------
W_ih, W_hh = rnn.weight_ih_l0, rnn.weight_hh_l0
b_ih, b_hh = rnn.bias_ih_l0, rnn.bias_hh_l0

h = torch.zeros(4) # the state starts at zero

bool(torch.allclose(outputs[0, -1], last[0, 0])))

title: Text Classification
heading: Why a plain RNN forgets, and what an LSTM does
text:
The hidden state is rewritten at every single word. Rewrite it forty times
and whatever was in it at the start is gone.

The vanishing gradient, in words

Training works backwards. The loss is computed at the end of the review,
and to discover that the first word mattered, that signal has to
travel back through every step in between. At each step it is multiplied
by the same two things: the derivative of tanh , which is never
greater than 1, and the recurrent matrix U . Multiply by
roughly the same factor forty times and one of two things happens.

Factor below 1 — vanishing

0.5 40 is about 10 −12 . The signal arrives as
nothing, the early weights never move, and the model simply never
learns that the beginning of the review existed.

Factor above 1 — exploding

1.5 40 is about 10 7 . One batch produces an
enormous update and the weights jump to nonsense. This half is easy to

1.5 40 is about 10 7 . One batch produces an

patch, and clip_grad_norm_ in our training loop is the
patch.

The vanishing gradient, measured

This is not a story — it is something you can print. Feed a 40-word
sequence in, send one signal back from the final state, and ask how much
of it reaches each input position.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

LENGTH, DIM, HIDDEN = 40, 32, 64

def gradient_by_position(cell):
"""How much does the final state still depend on the word at each position?"""
torch.manual_seed(0)
words = torch.randn(1, LENGTH, DIM, requires_grad=True)
_, state = cell(words)
hidden = state[0] if isinstance(state, tuple) else state # LSTM returns (h, c)
hidden.sum().backward() # one signal, sent back from the end

return words.grad[0].norm(dim=1) # one number per position

torch.manual_seed(0)
rnn = nn.RNN(DIM, HIDDEN, batch_first=True)
torch.manual_seed(0)
lstm = nn.LSTM(DIM, HIDDEN, batch_first=True)

# The standard trick: start the forget gate open. nn.LSTM stacks the gates as
# (input, forget, cell, output), so the forget bias is the second quarter.
torch.manual_seed(0)
open_lstm = nn.LSTM(DIM, HIDDEN, batch_first=True)
with torch.no_grad():
open_lstm.bias_ih_l0[HIDDEN:2 * HIDDEN].fill_(3.0) # sigmoid(3) ≈ 0.95

grads = {name: gradient_by_position(cell) for name, cell in
(("RNN", rnn), ("LSTM", lstm), ("LSTM, forget open", open_lstm))}

The point: an LSTM does not remove the vanishing
gradient. It gives the model a knob that can switch it off, and
lets training decide, per dimension and per review, when to turn it.
A plain RNN has no such knob.

What an LSTM adds

An LSTM adds a second vector, the
cell state , which travels from step to step almost
untouched — multiplied and added to, never passed through a weight
matrix. Three gates , each a small network producing
numbers between 0 and 1, decide what to erase, what to add, and what to
reveal.

The blue line is the cell state. Follow it across: it meets one multiplication and one addition, and nothing else. That straight path is what the gradient travels back along.

The two equations, term by term

f ⊙ cₜ₋₁
forget. A number near 1 keeps that dimension of the memory; near 0 erases it. This is the knob measured above
i ⊙ ĉ

i ⊙ ĉ
input. ĉ is the new candidate value, i decides how much of it to write
cₜ = f ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + i ⊙ ĉ
the whole update: scale what was there, add what is new. An addition, not a rewrite
hₜ = o ⊙ tanh(cₜ)

Compare with the RNN: there, h was both the
memory and the output, and every step overwrote it. Here the memory has
its own protected lane.

Batching: why padding is needed at all

The network is fastest when it processes many reviews at once, because
that turns per-word arithmetic into matrix multiplication. But a batch is
a tensor, and a tensor is a rectangle: every row must have the same
length. Reviews do not. So we pad each batch out to its longest review and

title: Text Classification
heading: From words to numbers
text:
tch is
a tensor, and a tensor is a rectangle: every row must have the same
length. Reviews do not. So we pad each batch out to its longest review and
pass the true lengths alongside.

Three decisions in collate

pad to the batch
not to a fixed width. A batch of short reviews stays narrow, so no work is wasted on a rectangle sized for the longest review in the dataset
pad with 0
index 0 is <pad> , and Embedding(..., padding_idx=0) keeps that row at zero and never trains it
keep the lengths
without them nothing downstream can tell a real word from filler

Reading: padding is a shape problem, not a modelling
idea. Everything that follows exists to undo it.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn

PAD = 0

class Recurrent(nn.Module):
"""Embedding -> RNN or LSTM -> Linear."""

def __init__(self, vocab_size, classes, kind="lstm", dim=100, hidden=128, dropout=0.3):
super().__init__()
self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim, padding_idx=PAD)
cell = nn.LSTM if kind == "lstm" else nn.RNN
self.rnn = cell(dim, hidden, batch_first=True)
self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)
self.out = nn.Linear(hidden, classes)

def forward(self, ids, lengths):

nine-word reviews it is exactly what you should expect.

Accuracy is the wrong metric for an ordered scale. It
charges the same penalty for calling a five-star review four stars as for
calling it one star. When classes have an order — ratings, severity levels,
grades — report the distance as well: mean absolute error, or the
within-one accuracy above. A model that is never more than one star off is
useful; its accuracy of 0.374 makes it sound useless.

And notice what is not the explanation. The test set is
balanced at 490 per class, so this is not the imbalance of the raw data
showing through. Five ordered classes on nine-word reviews is simply a
harder problem than two.

Theory · The honest summary

title: Text Classification
heading: What recurrence still cannot do
text:
It reads strictly left to right

When the model reaches емес it cannot go
back and revise what it thought about
жақсы . A bidirectional LSTM reads both ways
and helps, but it is two passes glued together, not a solution.

Everything squeezes through one vector

A forty-word review has to fit into 128 numbers before the classifier
sees anything. The longer the text, the more that bottleneck costs.

It cannot be parallelised

Step 20 needs the result of step 19. Words cannot be processed
simultaneously, which is exactly why training on very large corpora
became impractical.

Distance still costs

Gates slow the forgetting, they do not stop it. Linking word 2 to word
45 means carrying information through 43 updates.

LSTM →

Attention

Attention

The next lecture removes the loop entirely. Instead of passing information
along a chain, every word looks directly at every other word in one step —
which fixes the bottleneck, the distance penalty and the parallelism
problem at once. That is attention, and it is what Transformers are built
from.

title: Text Classification
heading: Knowledge check
text:
Five questions we answer together before finishing.

Question 1

What can an RNN represent that an average of word vectors cannot?

Show Answer

Order. The hidden state after
жақсы емес differs from the one after
емес жақсы ; the average is identical for
both, as measured at the top of this page.

Question 2

Why is rnn.weight_ih_l0 shaped (512, 100) when the hidden size is 128?

Show Answer

512 = 4 × 128. An LSTM computes four things at each step — the
forget, input and output gates plus the candidate value — and PyTorch
stacks their weight matrices into one.

Question 3

The LSTM's training loss keeps falling while test accuracy stops moving. What is happening, and what would you change?

Show Answer

Overfitting — 700 000 parameters against 8 000 short reviews. Options:
stop earlier, raise dropout, shrink the model, or give it more data.

text:
w Answer

Overfitting — 700 000 parameters against 8 000 short reviews. Options:
stop earlier, raise dropout, shrink the model, or give it more data.
We measured the last one: 40 000 reviews took it from 0.772 to 0.803.

Question 4

Why does starting from the Lecture 4 word2vec help so much in the first epoch?

Show Answer

83% of the parameters are the embedding table, and 5 743 of its 5 916
rows arrive already knowing which words behave alike. The network
starts from structure instead of noise: 0.785 after one epoch against
0.727.

Question 5

The score model is 0.374 accurate. Why is that not the most informative number to report?

Show Answer

The classes are ordered, and accuracy treats every mistake as equal.
The same model is within one star 70.4% of the time and off by three
or more only 12.2% of the time — which is what someone deciding
whether to use it actually needs to know.

Task 1 — Hidden size

Run --hidden 32, 128 and 512 on polarity. Does a bigger hidden state help?

Show Answer

Expect it to stop helping quickly and then hurt: more capacity with
the same 8 000 reviews means faster overfitting. Watch the gap
between training loss and test accuracy, not just the final number.

Task 2 — Bidirectional

Add bidirectional=True to the LSTM. Remember that the hidden state is now two vectors — how do you feed the linear layer?

Show Answer

Concatenate the last forward and backward states with
torch.cat([hidden[-2], hidden[-1]], dim=1) and make the
linear layer 2 * hidden wide. On nine-word reviews the
gain is usually small; say by how much.

Task 3 — Freeze the embeddings

Task 3 — Freeze the embeddings

With --pretrained, set embedding.weight.requires_grad = False. Better or worse, and why?

Show Answer

Freezing removes 83% of the parameters from training, so it overfits
far less but cannot adapt the vectors to sentiment. On a small
training set frozen often wins; on 40 000 reviews it usually loses.
Measure both.

Task 4 — max_len

Reviews are cut to 60 words. How many are actually affected, and what happens at --max-len 20?

Show Answer

The average review is about nine tokens and the longest is 271, so 60
cuts very few. That is itself the finding: this dataset gives a
recurrent model almost no length to work with.

Theory · The problem

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Before attention: one vector had to carry everything
text:
Attention was not invented for Transformers. It was invented in 2014 to
fix a specific, visible failure in machine translation — and the
failure is worth seeing before the fix.

The machine-translation system of the time was an
encoder–decoder RNN . One recurrent network reads the
source sentence word by word; its final hidden state is handed to a second
recurrent network, which writes the translation word by word. Take the
sentence we will use throughout this section:

Source · English
The cat sat on the mat

Target · Russian
Кошка сидела на коврике

The 2014 encoder–decoder. Six words go in, one vector comes out, and the decoder writes the whole translation from that vector alone.

What goes wrong, in order of severity

a fixed budget for a variable job

heading: Before attention: one vector had to carry everything
text:

What goes wrong, in order of severity

a fixed budget for a variable job
The context vector c has the same size for a four-word sentence and a forty-word one. The longer the sentence, the more meaning has to be squeezed into the same number of coordinates
the decoder cannot ask again
When it is about to write коврике , the useful evidence is the word mat . That word was read six steps ago and has since been overwritten five times. There is no way to go back and look
distance costs
Lecture 5 measured this: the gradient shrank ×0.48 per step. Information about The has to survive five rewrites to reach c
no parallelism
Step t cannot start until step t−1 finishes. Sentence length is also computation depth

The empirical symptom: translation quality of these

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Before attention: one vector had to carry everything
text:
rallelism
Step t cannot start until step t−1 finishes. Sentence length is also computation depth

The empirical symptom: translation quality of these
models fell off sharply as sentences got longer. Short sentences were
fine; long ones degraded, and they degraded in a characteristic way
— the beginning of the source was forgotten.

The idea that fixes it. Instead of forcing the decoder to
rely on one vector, keep all the encoder states
h1…h6 and let the decoder look back at whichever ones
are relevant for the word it is writing right now.

Bahdanau’s fix, 2014. Writing коврике , the decoder builds its own context vector by weighting the encoder states — and most of the weight lands on mat .

The word “attention” is descriptive, not metaphorical.
Those six numbers 0.03 … 0.71 are real
quantities inside the model, they sum to 1, and they are computed fresh for

Theory · The core idea

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: The intuition: relevance, then a weighted average
text:
For the current token, work out which other tokens are relevant, and
combine information from them in proportion to that relevance. That is the
entire mechanism. Everything else in this lecture is bookkeeping around it.

Attention lets each token build a new version of itself
by taking a weighted average of all the tokens in the sequence .
The weights say how relevant each other token is to this one ,
they sum to 1, and they are computed from the data rather than fixed in
advance.

The example we will keep coming back to

English

The animal didn’t cross the street because
it was tired.

A human reader resolves it without effort:
it is the animal. Nothing in the surface form
says so. The pronoun sits eight words after its referent, and if you change
one word — because it was too wide — the answer flips
to street . To build a useful representation of

one word — because it was too wide — the answer flips
to street . To build a useful representation of
it , the model must reach back and pull in the
meaning of animal .

What attention does to one token. The weights are the mechanism; the new vector for it is the product.

The seven questions, answered for attention

What problem does it solve?
Words that depend on each other can be arbitrarily far apart, and a recurrent state cannot hold everything on the way
What is the intuition?
Let each token ask the sequence a question and read back a blend of the answers, weighted by how well each token matches the question
What are the inputs?
One vector per token — the output of the previous layer, or the embeddings if this is the first layer
What operation happens?

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: The intuition: relevance, then a weighted average
text:
on
What are the inputs?
One vector per token — the output of the previous layer, or the embeddings if this is the first layer
What operation happens?
Score every pair, scale, softmax, then average the value vectors with those weights
What is the output?
One vector per token again, the same shape as the input — but now context-dependent
Why is it useful?
Any two tokens are one operation apart regardless of distance, and every position is computed in parallel
Where does it appear?
Three places in a Transformer: encoder self-attention, decoder masked self-attention, and decoder cross-attention

Keep this list. Every component introduced from here on
— the FFN, the residual, LayerNorm, positional encoding — will
be introduced by answering the same seven questions.

Theory · The three roles

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Query, Key and Value
text:
“How relevant is token j to token i ” is not a
single question, so a single vector per token cannot answer it. Attention
gives every token three vectors instead of one.

Query · what I am looking for

The token’s question. For
it , something like “which noun could
I be standing in for?”

Key · what I advertise

The token’s label, as seen by everyone else. For
animal , something like “I am a
singular animate noun.”

Value · what I hand over

The content that actually gets copied if this token is selected. For
animal , its meaning — which need not
look anything like its key.

Why key and value differ

Being findable and being useful are different jobs.
Tying them would force one vector to do both, and the model would lose
the freedom to advertise one thing and carry another.

The database analogy, and its limit. In a dictionary you

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Query, Key and Value
text:
to do both, and the model would lose
the freedom to advertise one thing and carry another.

The database analogy, and its limit. In a dictionary you
give a key, find the one matching entry, and get its value. Attention does
the same thing softly : your query is compared with every key, and
you get back a blend of all the values, weighted by match quality. There is
no winner and no lookup failure — every token always contributes
something, however little.

Where the three vectors come from

They are three linear projections of the same input. Nothing more
mysterious than three matrix multiplications:

Q = X W_Q K = X W_K V = X W_V

Q, K and V are three views of the same tokens. The matrices start random and are shaped entirely by training.

Every symbol in Q = X W_Q

Theory · One detail that is not a detail

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Why divide by √dₖ
text:
“For numerical stability” is the answer people repeat and it
explains nothing. Here is the actual argument, and then the measurement.

The argument in three steps

1. dot products grow with dimension
If q and k have dₖ independent components with mean 0 and variance 1, their dot product has mean 0 and variance dₖ . Its typical size is therefore √dₖ . At dₖ = 64 that is 8× larger than at dₖ = 1 , purely from the dimension
2. softmax is scale-sensitive
Softmax cares about differences between scores. Multiply all scores by 8 and a modest gap of 2 becomes a gap of 16, and e¹⁶ is nearly nine million times e⁰ . One token takes essentially all the weight
3. a saturated softmax has no gradient

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Why divide by √dₖ
text:
of 2 becomes a gap of 16, and e¹⁶ is nearly nine million times e⁰ . One token takes essentially all the weight
3. a saturated softmax has no gradient
Where the output is 1.000 and 0.000, the derivative of softmax is almost exactly zero. No gradient reaches W_Q or W_K, and the layer stops learning — permanently, since it cannot move away from where it is stuck

The fix: divide the scores by √dₖ ,
which cancels exactly the growth introduced by the dimension and returns
the scores to a range where softmax still has slope.

The same four scores, before and after dividing by √d. Scaling does not change which token wins — it changes by how much.

Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax( Q·Kᵀ / √dₖ ) · V

Read left to right, it is exactly the five steps you just computed by hand,
with steps 4 and 5 written as one product. Learn it as four verbs, not as a
string of symbols.

The four steps. Nothing here is a loop: every pair of positions is scored in one matrix multiplication.

# 2. scale, so the numbers stay in a range softmax can work with
scores = scores / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1))
# 3. turn into weights that sum to 1
weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)
# 4. take the weighted average of the values
out = weights @ V

Theory · The variant that built the Transformer

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Self-attention
text:
In Bahdanau’s translation model the queries came from the decoder and
the keys came from the encoder — two different sequences. Self-attention
is what you get when you point the mechanism at a single sequence.

Self-attention is attention where Q, K and V are all
computed from the same sequence. Every token queries the very
sequence it belongs to, itself included. Hence “self”.

English

The scientist published her paper because
she finished the experiments.

Three different tokens in this sentence need three different things.
her needs to know whose paper it is.
she needs its referent.
finished needs its object. One self-attention
layer computes all three at the same time, because every row of the weight
matrix is an independent decision.

One layer, three independent decisions. Each row of the attention matrix is computed from its own query and does not constrain the others.

What a token means before

The embedding of her is the same vector in
every sentence in the corpus. It encodes the word, not this use of it.

What it means after

The output vector for her is built mostly
from the value of scientist . Two sentences
with different referents give two different vectors for the same word.

This is the single most important consequence of the whole
lecture. After self-attention, a token’s representation is no
longer a property of the token — it is a property of the token
in this sequence . Lecture 4’s word2vec gave
банк one vector forever; self-attention gives it
one vector per sentence. That is the difference between a static embedding
and a contextual one, and it is why Lecture 7 can build BERT out of exactly

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: The kinds of attention, and how they differ
text:
Two things vary between attention variants: how the score is
computed , and where Q, K and V come from . Nothing
else. Here are both axes.

Axis 1 · How the score is computed

Three scoring functions. The Transformer picked the cheapest one and fixed its one weakness with a division.

Why the Transformer chose scaled dot-product

additive attention
score(q, k) = vᵀ tanh(Wₕq + Wₖk) . A one-hidden-layer network evaluated for every query–key pair. It works well and it handles queries and keys of different widths, but it cannot be written as a single matrix product, so on modern hardware it is far slower
dot-product attention
score(q, k) = q·k . No parameters at all, and the entire n×n score matrix is one matrix multiplication — the operation GPUs are built for. Its weakness is exactly the one we measured: at large d the scores blow up
scaled dot-product

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: The kinds of attention, and how they differ
text:
trix multiplication — the operation GPUs are built for. Its weakness is exactly the one we measured: at large d the scores blow up
scaled dot-product
score(q, k) = q·k / √dₖ . Keeps the speed, removes the weakness. The 2017 paper compared the two directly and found them equally accurate at small d , with additive attention ahead at large d — until the scaling was added

The lesson is not “dot products are better”.
It is that an operation which maps onto one matrix multiplication can be
scaled to billions of parameters, and one that cannot, cannot.

Bidirectional versus causal is the deepest split in the table.
A bidirectional encoder may use the right-hand context, so it builds the
best possible representation of a token — but it cannot generate,
because generating means not knowing what comes next. A causal decoder can
generate, and pays for it by never seeing the future. Every architecture in
section “families” below is a consequence of that one choice.

Theory · Masking

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Causal masking: hiding the future
text:
A model trained to predict the next token must never be shown that token.
With attention, “never shown” has a precise implementation.

Take I love deep learning . During training we
want all four next-token predictions computed in one pass — that
parallelism is the whole reason to use a Transformer. But position 2 must
predict deep while being able to see only
I love . Each position therefore gets its own
allowed window:

The causal mask. Row t has exactly t +1 blue cells — a good invariant to assert in your own code.

The mask, question by question

What problem does it solve?
Without it, predicting the next token is trivial: the token is right there in the input, and the model learns to copy it. Training loss falls to zero and the model generates nothing useful
Why −inf rather than 0?

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Causal masking: hiding the future
text:
right there in the input, and the model learns to copy it. Training loss falls to zero and the model generates nothing useful
Why −inf rather than 0?
Setting the score to zero would still leave weight e⁰ = 1 after softmax. Setting it to −inf gives e^(−inf) = 0 , an exact zero, and no gradient path
Why is training still parallel?
All n predictions are computed in one forward pass; the mask is what keeps them honest. This is the key efficiency difference from an RNN, which really must run n steps
Does generation use it too?
Yes, though at generation time there is no future to hide — the tokens simply do not exist yet. The mask matters most during training

Padding masks and causal masks are the same machinery.
Both write −inf into the score matrix before the softmax. They
differ only in which cells they choose, and a batched decoder applies both
at once.

Theory · More than one question at a time

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Multi-head attention
text:
One attention operation produces one set of weights per token, so it can
follow one kind of relationship. A sentence has several running at once.

English

The bank approved the loan because it
considered the applicant reliable.

To build a good vector for it , several different
relationships matter simultaneously, and each has a different answer:

Coreference

it → bank . Which noun am I standing for?

Subject–verb

it → considered . Which verb am I the subject of?

Local syntax

it → because . What clause am I inside?

Topic

it → loan . What is this sentence about?

A single softmax must compromise between these — it has one unit of
weight to distribute and four things to spend it on. The fix is to run
several attention operations in parallel, each in its own projection space,
and concatenate what they find.

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Multi-head attention
text:
things to spend it on. The fix is to run
several attention operations in parallel, each in its own projection space,
and concatenate what they find.

Eight heads of 64 dimensions, not one head of 512. The final projection Wₒ is what lets a token combine what different heads found.

Heads are not assigned roles. Nobody tells head 3 to track
coreference. Every head starts from random projections and is shaped only
by the gradient of the training loss. When researchers later inspect a
trained model and report “this head follows syntactic dependencies”,
they are describing something that emerged . Many heads turn out to
do nothing identifiable at all, and a well-known result is that a large
fraction of them can be pruned after training with little loss.

The dimensions, worked out

The original paper used d_model = 512 and
h = 8 heads, giving
dₖ = dₕ = 512 / 8 = 64 . That division is the

Architecture · The turn

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: From attention to the Transformer
text:
Until 2017 attention was an addition to a recurrent network: the
RNN did the sequence modelling, attention helped the decoder look back. Then
someone asked the obvious question.

What if we remove the recurrence entirely and build the
whole sequence model out of attention? The paper that did this was called
Attention Is All You Need , and the title is the argument.

Recurrence compared with attention

Property RNN / LSTM Self-attention

Path between two tokens up to n steps 1 step

Sequential operations n , cannot be parallelised 1

Work per layer n × d² n² × d

Word order built in absent — must be added

Memory for the score matrix none n² per head

The trade is explicit: attention gives up cheap scaling in sequence length
and built-in ordering, and buys a constant-length path between any two
tokens plus complete parallelism. On the hardware of 2017 — and much

and built-in ordering, and buys a constant-length path between any two
tokens plus complete parallelism. On the hardware of 2017 — and much
more so on the hardware of today — that trade was overwhelmingly worth
making. The two costs are fixable: word order is restored by adding a
positional signal, and the quadratic term is tolerable at the sequence
lengths people actually use.

Architecture · The bottom of the diagram

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: From a string to a matrix
text:
A Transformer consumes a matrix of floats. Getting a sentence into that form
takes three steps, and each one is a design decision.

Four steps from a string to one row of the input matrix X. Repeat for every token and you have (n, 512) .

The three steps, and what each decides

tokenization
Lecture 2 covered this. Modern Transformers use sub-word tokenizers (BPE, WordPiece, SentencePiece) rather than whole words, so there is no out-of-vocabulary problem — an unseen word is spelled out of familiar pieces. This matters enormously for Kazakh: кітаптарымыздан need not be its own vocabulary entry, it can be assembled from a root and suffixes
token ids
Each token becomes an integer index. The ids carry no meaning — id 8106 is not “more” than id 412. They are addresses, nothing else
embedding lookup

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: From a string to a matrix
text:
Each token becomes an integer index. The ids carry no meaning — id 8106 is not “more” than id 412. They are addresses, nothing else
embedding lookup
The embedding table is a learned matrix of shape (vocab, d_model) . Looking up an id is selecting a row. This is the same object as Lecture 4’s word2vec table, except it is trained jointly with the rest of the model instead of separately
positional information
Added, not concatenated. The next section explains why it is needed at all

Where the parameters are: at
30 000 × 512 the embedding table alone holds
15.4 million parameters — more than any single Transformer block. In
small models the embedding table is usually the largest thing in the file.

Architecture · The missing piece

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Attention cannot tell word order
text:
This is the flaw in everything above, and it is worth pausing on, because
the whole point of Lecture 5 was that order matters.

Two sentences, one bag of words
dog bites man

man bites dog

Look again at softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d)·V . No term
in it refers to a position. Permute the rows of X and every row of the
output is permuted the same way — the mechanism is
equivariant to reordering. To a bare self-attention layer, those two
sentences are the same input in a different order, and the representation it
builds for dog is identical in both. Without a
fix, a Transformer is a very expensive bag of words.

scores = vectors @ vectors.T / math.sqrt(vectors.size(-1))
return scores.softmax(dim=-1) @ vectors

def positional_encoding(length, dim):
position = torch.arange(length).unsqueeze(1).float()

Sinusoidal positional encoding

The original solution gives each position a fixed vector built from sines
and cosines at many frequencies:

PE(pos, 2i) = sin( pos / 10000^(2i/d) )
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos( pos / 10000^(2i/d) )

pos = which position in the sequence
i = which pair of dimensions
d = d_model

Like the digits of an odometer: the last digit changes every step, the first almost never. No two positions get the same combination.

table = torch.zeros(length, dim)

Architecture · The building block

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One encoder block, component by component
text:
Six pieces, in this order: multi-head self-attention, a residual, layer
normalisation, a feed-forward network, another residual, another layer
normalisation. Each one exists for a reason you can state in a sentence.

Attention moves information sideways between tokens; the feed-forward layer works on each token independently. Both are wrapped in a residual, so the block adds to its input rather than replacing it.

1 · Multi-head self-attention

What it is for: this is the only component in the entire
Transformer where information moves between positions. Delete it and you are
left with a model that processes each token in isolation — no context,
no relationships, no language. Every token reads every token and updates
itself with what it found.

2 · The residual connection

x ← x + Attention(x)

The sub-layer’s output is added to its input rather than

heading: One encoder block, component by component
text:
n and updates
itself with what it found.

2 · The residual connection

x ← x + Attention(x)

The sub-layer’s output is added to its input rather than
replacing it. Two consequences, both essential:

A residual turns a stack of replacements into a stack of corrections. The original vector always has an unobstructed route to the output — and the gradient has one back.

What the addition buys

gradient flow
The derivative of x + f(x) with respect to x is 1 + f′(x) . That 1 is a direct path: however small f′ becomes, the gradient still arrives. Without it, a 24-layer stack multiplies 24 small numbers together and the early layers never learn
information preservation
The block can only adjust the representation. If attention finds nothing useful for a token, outputting near-zero leaves the token as it was — a safe default. Without the residual, “do nothing” would have to be learned

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One encoder block, component by component
text:
ing useful for a token, outputting near-zero leaves the token as it was — a safe default. Without the residual, “do nothing” would have to be learned
the same trick you already know
Lecture 5’s LSTM cell state was added to rather than rewritten, for exactly this reason. Residual connections are that idea applied to depth instead of time

Measured on our own model: input norm 27.74, attention
output alone 5.65, after adding the residual 28.77. The block adjusts by
about one part in five; it does not overwrite.

3 · Layer normalisation

LayerNorm takes one token’s vector, subtracts its mean and divides by
its standard deviation, then rescales with two learned parameters. It
normalises across the features of one token — never across
the batch, and never across the sequence.

LayerNorm(x) = γ · (x − mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + ε) + β

mean, var computed over the d_model features of THIS token

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One encoder block, component by component
text:
, and never across the sequence.

LayerNorm(x) = γ · (x − mean(x)) / sqrt(var(x) + ε) + β

mean, var computed over the d_model features of THIS token
γ, β learned, one per feature

Why normalise at all

the problem
Every sub-layer changes the scale of its output a little. Stack 24 of them and the vectors arriving at the last layer may be a hundred times larger or smaller than what the layer’s weights were tuned for. Training becomes a moving target
the fix
Reset each token’s vector to mean 0 and variance 1 before the sub-layer reads it. Every layer then sees inputs on a predictable scale, whatever the layers below did
why not BatchNorm
BatchNorm normalises across examples in the batch, which makes each token’s representation depend on the other sentences it happened to be batched with, and breaks entirely at generation time with a batch of one. LayerNorm involves only the token itself

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One encoder block, component by component
text:
other sentences it happened to be batched with, and breaks entirely at generation time with a batch of one. LayerNorm involves only the token itself
γ and β
Normalising throws away scale and offset, which are sometimes useful. The two learned vectors let the model put back exactly as much as it wants

Pre-norm or post-norm? The 2017 paper normalised
after the residual addition. Practice moved to normalising
before the sub-layer, as in the diagram above, because it keeps
the residual path completely clean and lets deep models train without a
warm-up schedule. Almost every model since 2020 is pre-norm.

4 · The feed-forward network

FFN(x) = W₂ · σ(W₁x + b₁) + b₂

W₁: (512, 2048) expand
σ : ReLU in 2017, GELU or SwiGLU today
W₂: (2048, 512) project back

It is an ordinary two-layer MLP, applied to every position
independently and with the same weights . Token 3 and

W₂: (2048, 512) project back

It is an ordinary two-layer MLP, applied to every position
independently and with the same weights . Token 3 and
token 40 go through the identical network and never meet inside it.

Two orthogonal operations. Attention is the only one that crosses between columns; the FFN never does.

Architecture · Depth

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Stacking blocks: what actually changes with depth
text:
“Stack N of them” is a true but empty instruction. The question
worth answering is what is different about the representation at layer 12
compared with layer 1.

What deeper layers appear to represent. Treat the labels as a tendency observed in probing experiments, not as a specification anyone programmed.

What depth actually does

context widens
After one block a token has seen every other token — but only their pre-context versions. After two blocks it sees tokens that have themselves already seen everything. Information composes: layer 3 can use a relationship that only becomes visible once layer 2 has resolved something else
the representation drifts from the word
Early layers stay close to the embedding, so probes recover the identity of the word easily. Deep layers encode what the word is doing here , and the word itself becomes harder to recover
the shape never changes

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Stacking blocks: what actually changes with depth
text:
e identity of the word easily. Deep layers encode what the word is doing here , and the word itself becomes harder to recover
the shape never changes
(batch, tokens, 512) in, (batch, tokens, 512) out, for every block. That invariant is the entire reason stacking is possible, and why you can take 12 layers of a trained model and use only the first 6
each block has its own weights
Blocks are not shared. 12 blocks means 12 independent copies of the parameters — this is where a large model’s size comes from

Typical depths: the 2017 paper used 6 encoder and 6
decoder blocks; BERT-base 12; BERT-large 24; GPT-3 96. Depth, not width,
is usually the first thing scaled.

Architecture · The other stack

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: The decoder block
text:
The decoder produces the output sequence, one token at a time. Its block has
the encoder’s two sub-layers plus a third, and the third is the
interesting one.

A decoder block. Sub-layer 1 looks at what has been written; sub-layer 2 looks at what is being translated; sub-layer 3 thinks about it.

Masked self-attention asks: what have I written so far?

Q, K and V all come from the partial output. Writing
жақсы in
Мен машиналық оқытуды жақсы… , the model
needs to know it has already produced the object of the sentence.
Masked, because it must not see the words it has yet to write.

Cross-attention asks: what in the source is relevant now?

Q comes from the target, K and V from the encoder output. The token
being written queries the source sentence, and the source hands back the
part that matters — for
оқытуды , the English
learning .

heading: The decoder block
text:

being written queries the source sentence, and the source hands back the
part that matters — for
оқытуды , the English
learning .

Why both are needed, in one sentence each. Without masked
self-attention the decoder would not know what it has already said, and would
repeat itself or lose agreement. Without cross-attention it would not know
what it is translating, and would produce fluent text unrelated to the source.

Architecture · The bridge

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Cross-attention in detail
text:
Cross-attention is the same four steps with one change: the queries and the
keys come from different sequences. That single change is what connects two
languages.

self-attention Q = X W_Q K = X W_K V = X W_V
(target) (target) (target)

cross-attention Q = Y W_Q K = H W_K V = H W_V
(target) (encoder out) (encoder out)

A cross-attention map is a soft alignment between two languages — learned from parallel text alone, with no dictionary supplied.

Cross-attention, question by question

What are the inputs?
Two sequences: the decoder’s current representations Y of shape (m, d) , and the encoder’s output H of shape (n, d) . They need not have the same length
What is the score matrix?
Shape (m, n) — rectangular, not square. Row i is target token i ’s distribution over the source
Is it masked?

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Cross-attention in detail
text:
e same length
What is the score matrix?
Shape (m, n) — rectangular, not square. Row i is target token i ’s distribution over the source
Is it masked?
Not causally. The whole source is available from the start; there is nothing to hide. Only the source’s padding is masked
What is the output?
Shape (m, d) — one vector per target token, containing what that token pulled from the source
Where does it appear?
Only in encoder–decoder models: the original Transformer, T5, BART, Whisper. Decoder-only models such as GPT have no cross-attention at all, because they have no separate encoder

The historical circle closes here. This is precisely
Bahdanau’s 2014 idea from the start of the lecture — the decoder
looking back at all encoder states — expressed in the Q/K/V form and
computed with a matrix multiplication.

Architecture · End to end

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One sentence, all the way through
text:
Everything assembled, on one translation. Follow the eleven steps and you
have traced the entire architecture.

Source · English
I love machine learning.

Target · Kazakh
Мен машиналық оқытуды жақсы көремін.

The full loop. Steps 1–5 run once for the whole source; steps 6–11 run once per output token.

Three things the diagram makes visible

the encoder runs once
H is computed a single time and reused for every output token. Only the decoder loops. This is also the first hint of the KV cache idea discussed later
generation is autoregressive
Each new token is appended to the input and the decoder runs again. The model has no plan for the sentence; it has a probability distribution for the next token, repeatedly
the source and target lengths are independent

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One sentence, all the way through
text:
he model has no plan for the sentence; it has a probability distribution for the next token, repeatedly
the source and target lengths are independent
Four English tokens produced five Kazakh ones. Nothing in the architecture couples them — the decoder stops when it emits an end-of-sequence token

During training this is not a loop. The correct target
sentence is already known, so all output positions are computed in one
pass with the causal mask keeping each position honest. The slow
token-by-token loop happens only at generation time.

Architecture · The last layer

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: From a hidden vector to the next token
text:
The stack ends with one vector per position. Turning that into a word takes
exactly two operations, and they are the same two you have already seen.

Causal language modelling

The capital of Kazakhstan is ___

Illustrative probabilities. The mechanism is what matters: one linear layer per position, then a softmax over the whole vocabulary.

The output head, in detail

the linear layer
Shape (d_model, vocab) . Column w is a learned vector for word w , and the logit for w is the dot product of the hidden state with that column — the same similarity operation as attention scores, over the vocabulary instead of over the sequence
weight tying
Most models reuse the input embedding matrix, transposed, as this output matrix. It saves vocab × d_model parameters — 15 million in our example — and usually improves quality
softmax

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: From a hidden vector to the next token
text:
ing matrix, transposed, as this output matrix. It saves vocab × d_model parameters — 15 million in our example — and usually improves quality
softmax
The same function as inside attention, applied over the vocabulary axis instead of the sequence axis. Turns 30 000 arbitrary scores into 30 000 probabilities that sum to 1
choosing a token
Greedy takes the argmax; sampling draws from the distribution; temperature sharpens or flattens it before drawing; top-k and top-p truncate the tail first. This choice is decoding strategy, not architecture — Lecture 8 covers it
during training
No token is chosen at all. The cross-entropy loss reads off the probability assigned to the correct next token and pushes it up. Every position in every sequence contributes one such term

This is the entire objective of a language model.
Predict the next token, at every position, over and over, on enormous

This is the entire objective of a language model.
Predict the next token, at every position, over and over, on enormous
amounts of text. Everything a large model appears to know is a side effect
of getting good at that one task.

Architecture · Three descendants

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder–decoder
text:
The 2017 paper described one architecture. Almost everything since is one of
its two halves, or both. The choice follows from a single question: does the
model need to generate ?

Same block, three wirings. The difference is the mask and whether a second stack exists.

Encoder-only — BERT and its family

What it does

Reads the whole input with bidirectional attention and emits one
contextual vector per token. It cannot generate text, and does not try.

What it is for

Sequence classification (sentiment, intent), token classification (NER,
part of speech), sentence embeddings, retrieval, reranking,
extractive question answering.

Why bidirectional helps

To label банк in
Ол банкте отыр , the words after it are as
informative as the words before. A classifier has no reason to give up
half the evidence.

How it is trained

Not by next-token prediction — that would be trivial when you can

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder–decoder
text:
efore. A classifier has no reason to give up
half the evidence.

How it is trained

Not by next-token prediction — that would be trivial when you can
see the future. Instead words are masked out and reconstructed. Lecture
7 is entirely about this.

Decoder-only — GPT, Llama, Qwen, Gemma

One stack with causal masking, trained to predict the next token. This is
what essentially every modern large language model is, and the reasons it
won are worth stating explicitly:

Why decoder-only became dominant

the training signal is free and enormous
Any text is training data, and every token is a supervised example. A 1 000-token document yields 1 000 predictions. No labels, no parallel corpus, no annotation
one interface for every task

one interface for every task
Translation, summarisation, classification and question answering all become “continue this text”. An encoder–decoder needs a separate input and output convention per task; a decoder needs a prompt
simplicity scales
One stack, one mask, one objective. Fewer moving parts is a real advantage when you are training for months on thousands of accelerators
generation is native
The model is trained in exactly the mode it is used in. There is no mismatch between pretraining and deployment

The cost is real: a causal model builds worse
representations of the input than a bidirectional one, because it never
looks right. For pure classification on a fixed dataset, a BERT-size
encoder is often still the better and much cheaper tool.

Architecture · What changed since 2017

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: How modern LLM Transformers differ
text:
The skeleton you have just learned is still exactly right. Modern models
replace several components with better versions — each a local
substitution, none of them changing the shape of the story.

Five substitutions, one skeleton. Everything in blue at the bottom is what you have already learned, and it did not change.

Each change, and what it buys

pre-norm instead of post-norm
Normalise before the sub-layer, not after the residual addition. Keeps the residual path free of any normalisation, which lets very deep stacks train without a learning-rate warm-up. Essentially universal since GPT-2
RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm
Divide by the root-mean-square of the vector and skip the mean subtraction and the bias. Fewer operations, no measurable quality loss. A pure efficiency win, used by Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral
GELU and SwiGLU instead of ReLU

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: How modern LLM Transformers differ
text:
the bias. Fewer operations, no measurable quality loss. A pure efficiency win, used by Llama, Qwen, Gemma and Mistral
GELU and SwiGLU instead of ReLU
GELU is a smooth ReLU. SwiGLU splits the expansion into two branches, one acting as a learned gate on the other: FFN(x) = (Swish(xW₁) ⊙ xW₃)W₂ . It uses three matrices instead of two, so the hidden width is usually cut to about 2/3 to keep the parameter count level. Consistently a little better
RoPE instead of an additive position vector
Rotary Position Embedding rotates each query and key by an angle proportional to its position, inside the attention computation rather than at the input. The dot product between a rotated query and a rotated key then depends only on their relative distance — which is what attention actually needs, and what the sinusoidal table only approximated. It also extends to longer contexts far more gracefully

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: How modern LLM Transformers differ
text:
nce — which is what attention actually needs, and what the sinusoidal table only approximated. It also extends to longer contexts far more gracefully
MQA and GQA instead of full multi-head
Keep all h query heads, but share keys and values across them: one shared set (multi-query) or one per group of heads (grouped-query). Quality is nearly unchanged and the KV cache shrinks by the sharing factor — which is the binding constraint when serving long conversations
KV cache
Not an architecture change but the central inference trick. When generating token t +1, the keys and values of tokens 1… t are identical to what they were a step ago, so they are stored and reused. Generation goes from re-reading the whole prefix each step to appending one row. The cost moves from compute to memory, which is why GQA matters so much

What has not changed since 2017. Queries, keys and

network. Stacked identical blocks. Next-token prediction. Nine years of
intense work, and the core of the mechanism is exactly what you computed by

1 · Scaled dot-product attention

import math

import torch

def attention(query, key, value, mask=None):
"""query, key, value: (batch, heads, tokens, d_k)"""
scores = query @ key.transpose(-2, -1) # (batch, heads, tokens, tokens)
scores = scores / math.sqrt(query.size(-1))
if mask is not None:
scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))
weights = scores.softmax(dim=-1)
return weights @ value, weights # (batch, heads, tokens, d_k)

Line by line, against the formula

query @ key.transpose(-2, -1)
Q·Kᵀ — every query meets every key. transpose(-2, -1) swaps the last two axes only, leaving batch and head axes alone, so this is one batched matrix multiplication over all examples and all heads at once
/ math.sqrt(query.size(-1))

2 · Multi-head attention

import torch.nn as nn

class MultiHeadAttention(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, dim, heads):
super().__init__()
assert dim % heads == 0
self.heads, self.size = heads, dim // heads
self.query = nn.Linear(dim, dim) # W_Q
self.key = nn.Linear(dim, dim) # W_K
self.value = nn.Linear(dim, dim) # W_V
self.out = nn.Linear(dim, dim) # W_O

def split(self, x): # (b, t, dim) -> (b, heads, t, size)
batch, tokens, _ = x.shape
return x.view(batch, tokens, self.heads, self.size).transpose(1, 2)

def forward(self, x, mask=None):
q = self.split(self.query(x))
k = self.split(self.key(x))
v = self.split(self.value(x))

out, weights = attention(q, k, v, mask) # (b, heads, t, size)

batch, _, tokens, _ = out.shape

Q/K/V projections
Three nn.Linear(dim, dim) layers. Note that all heads are computed by one linear layer each, not h separate ones — the split into heads happens afterwards, which is why multiple heads cost nothing extra
reshape into heads

The function above, unchanged. Everything batched: (batch × heads) independent attention maps computed in one call

transpose(1, 2).reshape(...) is the exact inverse of the split. Concatenation is a reshape — no copying of meaning, just a different view of the same numbers
output projection
self.out is Wₒ . Without it the head outputs would sit in fixed, non-interacting slices of the vector; this layer is what lets a token combine what different heads found

The one subtlety: reshape rather than
view after the transpose, because the transposed tensor is no
longer contiguous in memory. This is the single most common runtime error
when people write this class from memory.

3 · A Transformer block

class Block(nn.Module):
"""pre-norm: LayerNorm -> sub-layer -> add"""

def __init__(self, dim, heads, hidden, dropout=0.1):
super().__init__()
self.attention = MultiHeadAttention(dim, heads)
self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
self.feed_forward = nn.Sequential(
nn.Linear(dim, hidden), # W_1: expand
nn.GELU(), # the non-linearity
nn.Linear(hidden, dim), # W_2: project back
)
self.dropout = nn.Dropout(dropout)

def forward(self, x, mask=None):
attended, weights = self.attention(self.norm1(x), mask)
x = x + self.dropout(attended) # residual 1
x = x + self.dropout(self.feed_forward(self.norm2(x))) # residual 2
return x, weights

class Transformer(nn.Module):
def __init__(self, vocab_size, classes, dim=128, heads=4, layers=2,
hidden=256, max_len=60, dropout=0.1):
super().__init__()
self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, dim, padding_idx=PAD)
self.register_buffer("positions", positional_encoding(max_len, dim))
self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
[Block(dim, heads, hidden, dropout) for _ in range(layers)])
self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(dim)

self.blocks = nn.ModuleList(
[Block(dim, heads, hidden, dropout) for _ in range(layers)])
self.norm = nn.LayerNorm(dim)
self.out = nn.Linear(dim, classes)

def forward(self, ids, pad_mask):
x = self.embedding(ids) + self.positions[:ids.size(1)] # (b, t, dim)
mask = pad_mask[:, None, None, :] # (b, 1, 1, t)
for block in self.blocks:
x, weights = block(x, mask)
x = self.norm(x)

# mean over the real tokens only — padding must not dilute the average
keep = (~pad_mask).unsqueeze(-1).float()
pooled = (x * keep).sum(1) / keep.sum(1).clamp(min=1) # (b, dim)
return self.out(pooled) # (b, classes)

The honest reading: this is a crude but sensible pattern,

The middle column is what cannot be parallelised. An RNN must finish step
t-1 before it can start step t, so a 256-word review is 256 waits deep.
Attention computes every position at once: one step, whatever the length.

The price is the last column. Doubling the length doubles an RNN's work
and quadruples attention's. At 256 words that is 65 536 pairs scored per
head per layer — which is why long documents need the efficient-attention
variants that came later, and why our 60-word cap is comfortable here.

This is the trade the Transformer makes. It buys a
constant path between any two words, and pays with work that grows as the
square of the length. At 60 words that is a bargain; at 60 000 it is the
reason a whole research area exists.

The fourteen questions this lecture must answer

Where does Q come from?
The token’s own input vector times the learned matrix W_Q . In cross-attention, from the target sequence
Where does K come from?
Each token’s input vector times W_K . In cross-attention, from the encoder output
Where does V come from?
The same vectors as K, times W_V . Same source as K, always
What does Q·Kᵀ mean?
A table of relevance: cell (i, j) is how well token i ’s question matches token j ’s advertisement
Why softmax?

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One token, all the way through
text:
rce as K, always
What does Q·Kᵀ mean?
A table of relevance: cell (i, j) is how well token i ’s question matches token j ’s advertisement
Why softmax?
To turn arbitrary real scores into non-negative weights that sum to 1, so the result is an average rather than an unbounded sum — and so that relative differences, not absolute magnitudes, decide the outcome
Why divide by √dₖ?
Dot products grow like √dₖ . Undivided, the softmax saturates to a hard 1/0 choice with a near-zero derivative and the layer stops learning. Measured: entropy 1.879 → 0.359
What does the output vector represent?
The token, rewritten to include what it found relevant elsewhere in the sequence. Same shape as the input, different contents
Why multiple heads?

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One token, all the way through
text:
nt?
The token, rewritten to include what it found relevant elsewhere in the sequence. Same shape as the input, different contents
Why multiple heads?
One softmax can express one relevance pattern. Several heads in separate subspaces can follow coreference, syntax and topic at once — and splitting a fixed width costs nothing
Why is positional information needed?
Attention is permutation-equivariant: we measured that shuffling the input just shuffles the output. Without positions, dog bites man and man bites dog are the same input
What happens inside one block?
Normalise, attend, add the residual; normalise, feed-forward, add the residual. Shape in equals shape out
Attention versus the FFN?
Attention mixes information across tokens with input-dependent weights. The FFN transforms each token independently with fixed weights, and holds two thirds of the parameters
What are residuals doing?

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: One token, all the way through
text:
t-dependent weights. The FFN transforms each token independently with fixed weights, and holds two thirds of the parameters
What are residuals doing?
Making every sub-layer a correction rather than a replacement, so the gradient has an unobstructed path through any depth and “change nothing” is the default
What is masking?
Writing −inf into chosen cells of the score matrix before the softmax. Causal masks hide the future; padding masks hide empty slots
What is cross-attention?
Attention with Q from one sequence and K, V from another. It is how a decoder reads an encoder, and how translation aligns two languages
How is the next token predicted?
Take the last position’s vector after the final block, project it to vocabulary size with one linear layer, softmax over the vocabulary, then pick or sample from that distribution

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Knowledge check
text:
Eight questions we answer together before finishing.

Question 1

What exactly was the bottleneck in an encoder–decoder RNN, and how does attention remove it?

Show Answer

The whole source sentence had to fit into one fixed-size context vector, and the decoder could never look back at the individual encoder states. Attention keeps all of them and lets the decoder compute a fresh weighted combination for every output token.

Question 2

Why is the value vector separate from the key?

Show Answer

Because being easy to find and being useful to read are different jobs. The key decides whether a token is selected; the value is what it contributes once selected. Tying them would force one vector to do both.

Question 3

In the hand-worked example, the row for жақсы was [0.284, 0.140, 0.576]. What do those three numbers mean, and why do they sum to 1?

Show Answer

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Knowledge check
text:
3

In the hand-worked example, the row for жақсы was [0.284, 0.140, 0.576]. What do those three numbers mean, and why do they sum to 1?

Show Answer

They are how much of жақсы ’s new vector is taken from each token’s value : 28.4% from қосымша , 14.0% from itself, 57.6% from емес . They sum to 1 because softmax normalises each row, so the output is a weighted average rather than an unbounded sum.

Question 4

We divide the scores by √dₖ. What breaks without it?

Show Answer

The softmax saturates. We measured it: at d = 64 the largest weight goes to 1.000 and the entropy collapses from 1.879 to 0.359. A saturated softmax has a near-zero derivative, so the layer stops receiving gradient and cannot recover.

Question 5

Shuffling the words gave an identical attention output. Why is that a problem, and what fixes it?

Show Answer

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Knowledge check
text:

Question 5

Shuffling the words gave an identical attention output. Why is that a problem, and what fixes it?

Show Answer

It means attention is a bag of words — the exact failure Lecture 5 existed to fix. Adding a distinct vector per position fixes it; we measured the outputs diverging by 1.166 once the positional table was added.

Question 6

A decoder block has three sub-layers. What would go wrong if you deleted the cross-attention? And the masked self-attention?

Show Answer

Without cross-attention the decoder cannot see the source at all — it would generate fluent but unrelated text, a language model rather than a translator. Without masked self-attention it would not know what it has already written, losing agreement and repeating itself.

Question 7

Attention gets the name. Where are most of the parameters?

Show Answer

title: Attention and Transformers
heading: Knowledge check
text:
it has already written, losing agreement and repeating itself.

Question 7

Attention gets the name. Where are most of the parameters?

Show Answer

In the feed-forward network. With the standard 4× expansion the FFN has about 2× the parameters of the attention sub-layer, and in a full model the embedding table is larger still. Attention decides what a token sees; the FFN is where most stored knowledge sits.

Question 8

Our Transformer scored 0.750, below TF-IDF’s 0.780. Is the architecture wrong?

Show Answer

No — it is data-starved. More epochs gave 0.749 and a smaller model gave 0.750, so it is neither undertrained nor oversized. Five times the data gave 0.787. Self-attention has to learn relationships from labels alone, and 8 000 short reviews cannot support that.

The observation that fixes it. Learning the language and

The observation that fixes it. Learning the language and
learning the task are two different jobs. The first needs enormous
amounts of text but no labels at all . The second needs labels
but, if the first job is already done, not very many. So do them
separately.

You have already seen this argument win once. Lecture 4
trained word2vec on all 134 368 unlabelled reviews and then handed the
vectors to the Lecture 3 classifier, which improved. Lecture 5 initialised

Theory · The core idea

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: Pretrain once, fine-tune many times
text:
Transfer learning splits training into two stages with completely different
economics. Understanding that asymmetry is most of understanding why the
field reorganised itself around it.

Pretraining is a public good: somebody spends weeks of GPU time, uploads the result, and every downstream task starts from it.

The two stages, side by side

what the data looks like
Pretraining: raw text, scraped, unlabelled, as much as you can find. Fine-tuning: your task’s labelled examples, however few you have
what the objective is
Pretraining: predict hidden words from their context. Fine-tuning: predict the label. The first is a proxy task nobody wants the answer to — it exists purely to force the model to learn the language
what it costs

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: Pretrain once, fine-tune many times
text:
ng: predict the label. The first is a proxy task nobody wants the answer to — it exists purely to force the model to learn the language
what it costs
Pretraining BERT-base in 2018 took 4 days on 16 TPUs. Fine-tuning it on our 8 000 reviews takes a few minutes on a laptop. The ratio is roughly four orders of magnitude
who does it
Pretraining: a research lab, once, and the weights are published. Fine-tuning: you, as often as you like
what changes in the weights
Pretraining: everything, from random. Fine-tuning: everything again, but gently — small steps from an already-good point rather than a search from nowhere

The name for the proxy task is self-supervision. The
labels are manufactured from the text itself by hiding part of it, so an
unlimited supply of supervised examples comes from data nobody had to
annotate. That single trick is what makes modern NLP possible.

Theory · The pretraining task

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: Masked language modelling
text:
To learn a language from raw text you need a question whose answer is
already in the text. BERT’s question is: I have hidden some
words — which words were they?

Masked language modelling. The label is the word that was removed, which makes every sentence in existence a free training example.

Why this particular task

it forces real understanding
To fill the gap in Бұл қосымша өте [MASK] екен the model must know what kind of word follows өте , that the sentence is about an app, and which adjectives Kazakh speakers use about apps. There is no shortcut
it can look both ways
This is the point of the name: B idirectional E ncoder R epresentations from T ransformers. The word екен after the gap is as useful as the words before it, and BERT is allowed to use it
the labels are free
Nobody annotated anything. The corpus is the label, hidden from itself
it is not next-token prediction

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: Masked language modelling
text:
BERT is allowed to use it
the labels are free
Nobody annotated anything. The corpus is the label, hidden from itself
it is not next-token prediction
A causal language model (Lecture 6, and Lecture 8) predicts the next token and may never look right. BERT gives up the ability to generate in exchange for seeing both sides — the trade-off from the previous lecture, made deliberately

Why 15%? Mask too little and each sentence teaches
almost nothing per forward pass, so pretraining takes forever. Mask too
much and too little context survives to make the gaps recoverable. 15% is
an empirical compromise from the original paper; later work found the
optimum is fairly flat and depends on model size.

The 80 / 10 / 10 detail

Of the tokens chosen for masking, BERT replaces only 80% with
[MASK] . 10% are replaced by a random word, and 10% are left
alone. This looks fussy and has a clear reason.

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: Masked language modelling
text:
or masking, BERT replaces only 80% with
[MASK] . 10% are replaced by a random word, and 10% are left
alone. This looks fussy and has a clear reason.

The model can never be sure whether the token it is looking at is right, so it has to form an opinion about every position rather than only the masked ones.

And the part that was dropped. The original BERT had a
second objective, Next Sentence Prediction: given two segments, are they
consecutive? It was meant to help question answering and inference. RoBERTa
later removed it and scored better , and essentially nothing since
has used it. This is a useful lesson about published recipes — parts of
them are guesses, and only later measurement separates the load-bearing
ideas from the decoration.

Theory · What BERT is

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT is the encoder half of Lecture 6
text:
There is no new architecture in this lecture. BERT is a stack of the
encoder blocks you built last time, plus three input conventions and a
pretraining objective.

Everything inside the dashed ENCODER box of Lecture 6’s full-architecture diagram, with [CLS] and [SEP] added and positions learned rather than sinusoidal.

The conventions worth knowing

[CLS]
A token prepended to every input whose only job is to accumulate a summary of the whole sequence. It has no meaning of its own; it is a place for the model to put an answer. Lecture 6 used mean pooling instead — both work, and [CLS] is the convention here because the pretrained weights were trained with it
[SEP]
A separator, so that two sentences can be fed as one input. This is what makes BERT usable for pair tasks: entailment, similarity, question answering over a passage
segment embeddings

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT is the encoder half of Lecture 6
text:
can be fed as one input. This is what makes BERT usable for pair tasks: entailment, similarity, question answering over a passage
segment embeddings
A third embedding table with exactly two rows, marking “this token belongs to sentence A” or “to sentence B”
learned positions
Not the sine table of Lecture 6 but a plain embedding table indexed by position, with 512 rows. Simpler, and the reason BERT cannot read anything longer than 512 tokens
WordPiece
A sub-word vocabulary of 30 000 entries, or 119 547 for the multilingual version. The next section shows what it does to Kazakh

The two sizes from the paper: BERT-base is 12 blocks,
12 heads, d_model = 768 , 110 M parameters — deliberately
matched to GPT-1 so the comparison was fair. BERT-large is 24 blocks,
16 heads, d_model = 1024 , 340 M parameters.

The same word, three vocabularies. A tokenizer that fits the language turns one word into its actual morphemes; one that does not turns it into debris.

Why the split matters

fragments are harder to learn from
If кітап is a single token, every sentence containing any form of “book” contributes to the same embedding. If the root is split differently depending on the suffix, that evidence is scattered across unrelated pieces
more pieces means less context

text:
mbedding. If the root is split differently depending on the suffix, that evidence is scattered across unrelated pieces
more pieces means less context
BERT’s limit is 512 positions. A tokenizer that needs six pieces per word fits a third as much text as one that needs two — and attention cost grows with the square of the length
the vocabulary is frozen
You inherit whatever the pretraining team chose. This is the one part of a pretrained model you genuinely cannot fix by fine-tuning
bigger is not automatically better
kaz-RoBERTa has a 52 000-entry vocabulary against XLM-R’s 250 002 and still splits Kazakh better, because all 52 000 entries are spent on one language instead of a hundred

A practical rule: before choosing a pretrained model for
a low-resource language, tokenize a few hundred words of your own data and
count the pieces per word. It takes two minutes and predicts a surprising

Theory · The second stage

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: What fine-tuning actually does
text:
Fine-tuning is a small idea with a few counter-intuitive details. The idea:
throw away the pretraining head, bolt on a new one, and keep training
— gently.

Two numbers worth holding together: 177 million weights arrive already trained, and 1 538 arrive random.

The details that are not obvious

everything trains, not just the head
The natural guess is to freeze the encoder and train only the new layer. It works, but not nearly as well — we measure the gap below. Letting the gradient reach all twelve blocks lets the representation itself adapt to the task
the learning rate is tiny
2e-5 here, against 3e-4 for the from-scratch model in Lecture 6 — about fifteen times smaller. You are starting from a good point and must not blow it away. Learning rates above about 1e-4 routinely destroy a pretrained model in the first few hundred steps
two to four epochs, not fifty

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: What fine-tuning actually does
text:
t not blow it away. Learning rates above about 1e-4 routinely destroy a pretrained model in the first few hundred steps
two to four epochs, not fifty
The original paper recommends 2–4 and that advice has held up. More epochs on a small dataset overfit quickly, because a 177 M-parameter model can memorise 8 000 short reviews without difficulty
warm-up and decay
The learning rate rises from zero over the first ~10% of steps and then decays linearly. The warm-up protects the pretrained weights while the random head is still producing nonsense gradients
the result is a separate model per task
Fine-tuning produces a new 177 M-parameter checkpoint. Three tasks means three copies. This is the cost that later methods — adapters, LoRA, prompting — exist to avoid, and Lecture 10 returns to it

Catastrophic forgetting is the thing to fear. Too large a

Catastrophic forgetting is the thing to fear. Too large a
learning rate, or too many epochs on too little data, and the model
overwrites the general language knowledge that made it valuable. The
symptom is training loss near zero and test accuracy worse than a linear
model. The defences are all conservative: small steps, few epochs,
warm-up.

Theory · The family

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT’s descendants, and what each one changed
text:
BERT was published in 2018 and immediately became a platform. Everything
below keeps the encoder stack and changes one thing: the data, the
objective, the parameter budget, or the size.

RoBERTa — the same model, trained properly

What changed

Ten times the data (160 GB against 16 GB), much longer training,
larger batches, dynamic masking — a fresh mask every epoch instead
of one fixed at preprocessing — byte-level BPE with 50 000
entries, and no Next Sentence Prediction .

What it showed

The architecture was never the bottleneck: BERT had simply been
undertrained. RoBERTa-base beats BERT-large on several GLUE tasks with
fewer parameters. “Robustly optimised” is the whole
contribution, and it was a large one.

DistilBERT and TinyBERT — the same knowledge, smaller

A 110 M-parameter model is awkward to serve: it is slow on CPU, too big for

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT’s descendants, and what each one changed
text:
was a large one.

DistilBERT and TinyBERT — the same knowledge, smaller

A 110 M-parameter model is awkward to serve: it is slow on CPU, too big for
a phone, and expensive at scale. Distillation trains a small
student to imitate a large teacher .

Knowledge distillation. The teacher’s soft probabilities carry more information per example than the correct answer alone, which is why the student learns so efficiently.

The two distilled models by name

DistilBERT
Six blocks instead of twelve, each initialised from every second block of the teacher. 66 M parameters, about 40% smaller and 60% faster, and it keeps roughly 97% of BERT’s GLUE score. Trained with three losses at once: ordinary MLM, the distillation loss against the teacher’s distribution, and a cosine loss pulling the student’s hidden states towards the teacher’s
TinyBERT

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT’s descendants, and what each one changed
text:
y MLM, the distillation loss against the teacher’s distribution, and a cosine loss pulling the student’s hidden states towards the teacher’s
TinyBERT
Goes considerably further. It distils not only the output distribution but the attention matrices and hidden states of intermediate layers, and it does so twice: once on general text, then again on the specific task with augmented data. The 4-layer, 312-dimension version is 14.5 M parameters — about 7.5× smaller and 9.4× faster than BERT-base — while retaining around 96% of its GLUE score
MiniLM
Distils the attention distributions themselves, self-attention value-relations included, and is the approach behind the small multilingual models in our comparison table

The honest caveat on all distillation numbers:
“97% of the performance” is an average over GLUE, which is
English and mostly easy. On a harder or lower-resource task the gap is

stillation numbers:
“97% of the performance” is an average over GLUE, which is
English and mostly easy. On a harder or lower-resource task the gap is
usually wider. We measure our own below rather than quoting theirs.

Three of those deserve a sentence more

ALBERT — small in storage, not in time
It shares one set of block weights across all twelve layers and splits the embedding matrix into two smaller ones. 12 M parameters against 110 M sounds dramatic, and the file really is that small — but it still runs twelve blocks at inference, so it is not faster. It is the one model in this table whose headline number is routinely misread
ELECTRA — a better use of every example

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT’s descendants, and what each one changed
text:
inference, so it is not faster. It is the one model in this table whose headline number is routinely misread
ELECTRA — a better use of every example
Instead of masking, a small generator substitutes plausible words and the main model decides, for every token , whether it was replaced. BERT learns from 15% of positions; ELECTRA learns from 100%. ELECTRA-small reaches GPT-level GLUE scores with roughly 1/30 of the compute, which makes it the strongest choice when the pretraining budget is small
DeBERTa — content and position, separately

title: BERT and Fine-tuning
heading: BERT’s descendants, and what each one changed
text:
with roughly 1/30 of the compute, which makes it the strongest choice when the pretraining budget is small
DeBERTa — content and position, separately
Each token carries two vectors, one for what it is and one for where it is, and attention is computed from content-to-content and content-to-position terms separately rather than from one summed vector. It was the first model to pass the human baseline on SuperGLUE, and DeBERTa-v3 — which adds ELECTRA-style pretraining — is still a very strong encoder today

Where the specialised models fit. Beyond the general
family there are domain models (BioBERT, SciBERT, FinBERT) and
language models (RuBERT, and for us
kaz-roberta-conversational ), all built by continuing
pretraining on text from one field or one language. When your data looks
like theirs, they usually win.

Lecture 6 wrote MultiHeadAttention , Block and Transformer by hand. Here from_pretrained replaces all of it — and it is worth remembering, while typing that one line, that it is loading exactly the architecture you built
the tokenizer is not ours

place. If you are serving this model, that is a 3.3× difference in
size and speed for a difference in accuracy you cannot measure.

The honest summary of two results. Pretraining is not a
uniform multiplier. On a task with real signal that a model has to learn
the language to extract, it is transformative. On a task whose difficulty
is irreducible ambiguity in the labels, it moves almost nothing — and
a careful practitioner reports the second result as loudly as the first,
because the alternative is promising a stakeholder an improvement that the
data cannot deliver.
